Developing robotic dexterous grasps for diverse objects poses a significant challenge, particularly given the vast number of possible grasps for each object, and further complicated by the need to accurately predict stable points despite potential simulation inaccuracies. To tackle this problem, we collected simulated data on 1026 grasps for 206 objects. Our collection process involved selecting dexterous grasps from a wide range of possibilities and validating them through both simulation and actual grasps to ensure accuracy. To address the disparity between simulated and real-world conditions, we applied transfer learning, utilizing pre-trained policy networks from a whole-object approach, which allowed us to collect large amounts of data in virtual environments. Our experiments using a seven-jointed Franka robot arm confirmed the effectiveness of our data collection approach, which achieved 90% accuracy in the most challenging 90% of scenarios when compared to existing methods. Our complete dataset, known as DexGraspNet, can be accessed at https://sites.google.com/view/dexgraspnet. With the integration of a novel evaluation method that accounts for multiple grasps and their associated probabilities, as well as pre-trained models for both EM-Greedy and DexNet, the dataset enables accelerated development of robotic dexterous grasps. Our proposed evaluation method is distinct from previous approaches, which typically measure performance using the success rate, as it provides a clearer picture of both precision and generalization by assessing the average probability of achieving a successful grasp beyond just the top-ranked prediction. Furthermore, the pre-trained models, which are based on policies trained using DexNet, have been adapted for fine-tuning on the DexGraspNet dataset and subsequent downstream tasks. To facilitate future research, the entire dataset, including data collection methods, evaluation procedures, and pre-trained models, is available for download at https://sites.google.com/view/dexgraspnet. Our goal is to make the dataset widely accessible to the research community in order to accelerate development of robotic dexterous grasps. What is particular about this research is that it highlights the need for accurate evaluation methods in robotic dexterous grasps, which is a critical component for evaluating whole-object to grasp object transitions. To rectify the existing disparity between simulated and real-world success rates, the proposed evaluation method provides a more comprehensive understanding of precision and generalization by assessing success rates for the top 98% of grasps. Our research also demonstrates the effectiveness of transfer learning in robotic dexterous grasps, which is a critical component for collecting whole-object dexterous grasps

For accurate assessment of body anatomy via MRI scanning, it's crucial to account for respiratory variations. Consequently, four-dimensional (4D) turbo spin-echo (TSE) sequences have emerged as a preferred method to capture these dynamics. Nevertheless, the requirement for manual breath-holding can result in substantial scanning time, limiting its feasibility. Therefore, employing rapid, unfeasible R-Artificial Intelligence (RAI) sequences to acquire hundreds of breathing cycles at the expense of motion sensitivity is an alternative approach. Subsequent application of motion correction algorithms can improve image quality. Our objective was to evaluate the efficacy of such a strategy using a database of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) scans. By combining 4D TSE with motion correction, we obtained comparable results, suggesting only 25% more scanning time of the initial RAI scan was necessary to produce equivalent image quality. Notably, the four-dimensional method allowed for the quantification of kidney organ function metrics, such as renal volume and glomerular filtration rate, similar to conventional three-dimensional (3D) TSE. Our findings demonstrate that the integration of rapid RAI sequences with motion correction provides an efficient solution to acquire high-quality 4D images with minimal additional scanning time. This strategy could potentially broaden the application of MRI for assessing vascular diseases using time-efficient methods. The main goal of model compression is to reduce the size of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) while minimizing their performance loss. Recently, knowledge distillation is known to generate compressed models with smaller performance losses in comparison to traditional model compression techniques. However, current distillation methods do not take into account the data flow of the compressed models, leading to discrepancies between the compressed models and the original DNNs they are based on. In this research, we introduce incompressing distillation (Indistill), a new method for model compression that preserves data flow. The results reveal that Indistill takes fewer steps to reach a high compression rate and maintains the same level of accuracy as regular distillation for the same number of steps on various tasks, such as image classification for low compression rates. The research also indicates that a combination of Indistill and traditional model compression can further improve the accuracy of the compressed models. The source code is available online. This research investigated the effects of non-resident grazing in drylands, focusing on how seasonal patterns influence the dynamics of plant species. Our model revealed that although non-resident grazing leads to fewer total grazing activities during the year, its impact on ecosystems is similar to that of resident grazing. This is because seasonal patterns can create fluctuations in plant populations and lead to cycles of growth and decline. Furthermore, our analysis indicated that a higher capital investment in infrastructure by grazers tends to benefit the ecosystem, driving plant populations towards stability. This benefit, however, only persists if the capital investment meets a certain minimum threshold, necessitating further investigation into the spatial movement patterns of grazers and dryland ecology. Such knowledge could be gained by incorporating more context and properties of non-resident and resident grazing into the models, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of their impacts and their implications for the dryland ecosystem. Simultaneously, our model showed that a higher capital investment in infrastructure by grazers can benefit the ecosystem, but this benefit depends on the grazing strategy and seasonal patterns. Therefore, it is crucial to address the question of how grazers operate during the grazing season, influencing the dynamics of plant species and variability in dryland ecosystems. Researchers suggest developing more nuanced mathematical models that integrate the inherent variability in drylands and the differing grazing strategies of non-resident and resident grazing, despite their equivalent total impact on the ecosystem. This analysis could further reveal how non-resident grazing influences the dynamics of dryland ecosystems, particularly through its effects on resource variability and the coexistence of multiple plant species. Consequently, our model suggests that a higher total impact by non-resident grazing does not necessarily translate to greater within-population variability, but rather indicates a broader effect due to the spreading of grazing activities over a longer duration. Therefore, it would be beneficial for future studies to investigate and address the question of how non-resident grazing's sporadic and scattered pattern influences the dryland ecosystem compared to resident grazing's more continuous and predictable foraging methods. Researchers could then develop a more detailed understanding of how non-resident grazing's frequency and distribution impact the dryland ecosystem, particularly through modeling studies that integrate the context and properties of non-resident grazing, ultimately requiring a more nuanced mathematical modeling approach that can capture the inherent ecological and spatial variability in drylands. By developing such models, future researchers can delve deeper into the dryland ecosystem, exploring how non-resident grazing's frequency and distribution affect the coexistence of multiple plant species and the overall dryland ecosystem stability. As cutting-edge technology integrates quantum principles into modern networks, engineers must consider the implications of quantized data to avoid unforeseen consequences. A recent example illustrates this challenge, demonstrating how an apparent benefit of quantizing data may actually facilitate its reconstruction from partial information, compromising security. A renowned physicist points out that this vulnerability arises from properties of wave functions, while a leading financial firm shows similar issues in its experimental quantum stock trading program on the cloud, potentially allowing rivals to exploit market disparities. These instances highlight the importance of distinguishing between different types of data and their encoding methods when utilizing quantum computing resources. Moreover, several potential solutions to address these vulnerabilities are discussed. A prequel to this analysis was previously provided as a response to a question on Quora. Abstractive condensation generates a summary by abstracting key information from a full text, but current methods struggle when the summary contains entities not present in the full text, leading to inaccurately summarized information. To overcome this issue, we introduce an entity prompt approach, where models can acquire and utilize entity representations from full texts to accurately handle summaries containing unseen entities. Through this approach, our semi-supervised method significantly improves the performance of abstractive condensation, outperforming previous methods on benchmark datasets in ROUGE metrics. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the acquired entity prompts and findings, providing valuable insights for the development of future condensation methods. The code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/AllanLin/aPC-EPT.

Notably, the proof does not rely on the standard methods of vector calculus used in the theory of differentiable functions of higher dimension. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the applicability of the obtained results to newly establishing new function spaces of differentiable mappings between infinite-dimensional spaces and proves key properties of functions belonging to these novel spaces. The results are illustrated by several examples that demonstrate the challenges associated with the differentiability of functions of higher dimension, without the use of vector calculus. Additionally, the study provides a new definition for the derivative of a function of higher dimension, under certain conditions, and investigates its relationship with the traditional Banach space defined by Djene and Vetro, revealing an equivalence that holds without additional requirements. Finally, the study delves into the relationship between the different types of derivatives that have been proposed in the literature and establishes that they are equivalent under the conditions of the traditional Banach space defined by Djene and Vetro. However, it is found that this equivalence does not necessarily hold for all functions of higher dimension, without additional requirements. Deep learning's success in robot perception and autonomy can be attributed to pre-trained models developed from widely available large-scale datasets. Traditionally, pre-training has focused on object recognition, but our study explores whether training on depth estimation alone offers advantages for subsequent semantic segmentation tasks. We investigated the depth segmentation task, which combines both depth and semantic labels in a single dataset, to determine the efficacy of pre-training on depth maps for subsequent semantic segmentation. Our results indicate that pre-training on the Datasettenholtz dataset, a collection of datasets with consistent domains and domains, outperforms traditional object recognition methods. However, this advantage was not observed in the CrossDomain dataset, which comprises datasets with distinct domains and climates. We found that pre-training on the crossdomain dataset led to slower convergence of subsequent tasks and similar task performance compared to pre-training from scratch. In contrast, a baseline model pre-trained on depth maps but not fine-tuned demonstrated improved task understanding and faster convergence, although the difference in performance and convergence speed was not significant. A thorough investigation of our findings reveals that the results from depth estimation and semantic segmentation are influenced by the same underlying factors. These factors can be categorized into two main groups: (a) the task's ability to gather informative gradients during pre-training due to the task's difficulty and prior knowledge, and (b) the task's ability to help the model develop generalized low-level features through statistical pattern analysis in dataset areas with minimal label noise. Our study provides an in-depth analysis of these two categories, enabling readers to comprehend how different tasks impact the development of low-level features in deep neural networks. Moreover, our study offers recommendations for forming a suitable dataset for pre-training, thereby enhancing both task understanding and convergence speed. One significant issue affecting the performance of parallel evolutionary algorithms in parallel computing environments is the variability in processing times. This arises from differences in algorithm operation, system load, and system configuration. As a result, algorithms that run in parallel may not utilize computational resources fairly, leading to an advantage for the agent (individual) that is evaluated next. Research suggests that this processing delay can substantially reduce the performance of evolutionary algorithms even further. To address this processing delay in multi-objective evolutionary algorithms, we present an innovative approach that prioritizes parent selection based on the frequency of evaluations rather than the time taken for evaluation. In this frequency-oriented parent selection, we group and analyze the evaluations by taking the total number of evaluations performed at regular intervals, while leveraging the capability of asynchronous computing to minimize processing delays. Computational experiments are conducted using five test functions in three MOEA/D variants in a parallel computing environment with up to 40 processes over three time intervals. Compared to the traditional time-oriented parent selection, our proposed approach results in better solution quality, especially for high computational intensities. Overall, our innovative selection strategy achieves a 47.8% reduction in the coefficient of variation of objective space distribution, thereby providing better fairness and use of computational resources. In addition, the solution quality obtained using frequency-oriented parent selection is found to be more consistent, resulting in better robustness in the presence of processing delays. Consequently, this strategy can enhance the performance of evolutionary algorithms even further when employed in parallel computing systems. In a regular triangular lattice, when two adjacent triangles share an edge, it creates a specific angle of 60 degrees. This topic explores the possibility of forming triangles within this grid, starting with a basic triangle and using smaller copies of it to build larger combinations. It involves counting the number of these larger triangles in a space occupied by the initial triangle and any subsequent additions made to it. An initial conjecture proposed that this number must always be 1. While this holds true for small combinations, a higher number can be attained by adding enough smaller triangles to a single initial triangle. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that the ultimate outcome of these combinations can be any positive integer greater than 1. This conclusion was reached by imagining the process through a 'demonstration without words,' which visually illustrates the varying outcomes and their patterns. An underlying statement of Euler's oddness has also been discovered, supporting the conjecture that triangular numbers must always be odd. Once the main issue was fully understood, proof for the conjecture had become its own demonstration of the answer. This method of work also uncovered further questions about the patterns of these combinations and their potential double identity in relation to two distinct values, one for individual combinations and another for their total sum. In light of these findings, further research is recommended to unlock a deeper understanding of these double identity patterns. Unsupervised inductive tests are used to assess the interpreter's ability to generalize information about GNN parameters. An experimental investigation into the interpreter's properties reveals limitations in its ability to discover and analyze multiple factors, such as the impact of individual parameters and feature interactions. This research also explores alternative configurations for the interpreter, aiming to expand its capabilities. In the naming game model with migrating agents, agents know their own languages but can only learn the language of others through social interaction. Our previous study revealed that langauge learning in this model is an extremely complex task. To further explore this phenomenon, we conducted additional simulations with a larger number of agents and more migration routes, and obtained new insights that confirm our previous findings. We also made a key discovery that suggests languages may become socially established, but it is highly unlikely that all agents will use the same language within a specified timeframe. This led us to create a metric to measure the linguistic consistency of the system. Based on this consistency metric, we defined a state of complete consistency where all agents speak the same language, and a partially consistent state where multiple distinct languages are used across different groups. Our results show that the system spends most of its time in the partially consistent state. We calculated the mean distribution of languages at the end of each simulation and used it to create a histogram that represents the system's language setup. This allows us to establish a linguistic consistency pattern. We hope that our study promotes further research in this area by encouraging others to replicate our results and explore the general patterns that emerge. Our long-term goal is to create a simulation and conduct a comprehensive analysis that covers a broad spectrum from small to large agent populations. This paper presents an innovative approach to blind image restoration issues, such as blind deblurring and blind demosaicking. It breaks down these complex problems into two simpler parts: identifying the blurring effect on a single pixel and estimating the intensity of that pixel. To achieve this, we utilize the Kernel Mixture Model (KMM) to create a kernel dictionary that approximates any given point in a higher-dimensional space. By selecting appropriate kernel bases and evaluating the probability distributions for each pixel's intensity, we develop low-resolution image generation networks that produce the blurred image. Then, we utilize the learned kernel dictionary for each pixel to create a solution for the restoration task. Our method demonstrates superior results and faster processing speed compared to current techniques. Furthermore, it can also be used for other blind image restoration problems. Hoare logic, a proven mathematical technique for assessing program reliability, has been extended through the creation of Natural Hoare Reasoning, a groundbreaking method.  This innovation enables the formal verification of programs written in high-level languages like C, using natural language statements that describe a program's input and output data without referencing specific implementation details. Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as stateless services utilizing a distributed ledger or cluster-level consensus for operations. Existing consensus research has primarily focused on either stateful or stateless systems, despite both being important for different applications. A recent proposal by Canopus addresses this gap by providing a framework for constructing both stateful and stateless consensus protocols. In this research, we address several limitations of Canopus by introducing RCanopus, a variant designed to withstand various failure modes and Byzantine faults. By integrating the Consensus with Chiou and Burckhardt's work and incorporating the capabilities of Randomized Consensus from Burckhardt et al., RCanopus achieves O(n^2) message complexity in the worst-case scenario, with an improved failure resilience and ability to operate under adverse conditions. Additionally, RCanopus allows for the creation of both stateful and stateless consensus protocols. By building upon RCanopus, we achieve new results, including the creation of a new stateless consensus protocol for distributed ledger applications. Finally, we demonstrate that RCanopus's existing and new protocols are applicable to various use cases, such as Distributed Ledger, Stateful, and Stateless Consensus. An evaluation reveals that these protocols outperform the DLEQ and Speculator protocols, previously developed for Distributed Ledger use cases. In particular, we verify the performance benefits of our protocols through testing on 20 unique failure configurations. Canopus's existing and new protocols are available for public evaluation at canopus.io/f, with failure configuration testing accessible at canopus.io/f/testing. In this research, we have contributed towards the creation of a resilient consensus framework capable of handling various failure modes and Byzantine faults. By making RCanopus's source code open-source, we intend for our framework to be widely adopted and utilized in future consensus protocol development. A key aspect of this work is the establishment of the Canopus Distribution (CD), a unique failure distribution, enabling open-source and generalizability in this research field. A related CD paper is currently in development for publication.

Our investigation introduces the new concept of maximizing the number of clicks under a given sequence. This requires an adaptive strategy as the length of the sequence grows exponentially with $n$, making this problem challenging. A solution for the one-dimensional case illustrates the complexity and inspires the first generalization - any valid sequence can be maximized in $O(n^2)$ clicks. Additionally, we identified the lower click limit for any sequence: $n^2 - n + 1$. Furthermore, we observed that sequences requiring $n$ or more clicks are capable of being optimized in $O(n^3)$ clicks. As a result, the upper click limit for these sequences is at most $n^3 + n^2$. These outcomes not only contribute to the existing body of work in Lights Out but also establish the upper limit for the maximum clicks problem. Moreover, our investigation into Lights Out on an $n$-dimensional cube revealed new concepts and insights, particularly that maximizing the number of clicks under an Echelon sequence is achievable in $O(n^4)$ clicks. Ultimately, the maximum clicks problem on an $n$-dimensional cube has a lower click limit of $3n^4/2 + n^3$. Alongside these core contributions, the maximum clicks problem also sheds light on the long-standing open question of determining whether the Lights Out problem is solvable through first-order logic. Our investigation demonstrates that any sequence can be optimized using first-order logic with the ability to count, as well as the ability to express reachability and the closure of a set of cells. Moreover, our work provides a generalization - any sequence can be optimized using first-order logic with the ability to count and a limited number of reachability and closure assertions. This finding reveals that the maximum clicks problem does not hold any significant insights for the logic-based investigation but contributes to the existing body of work in Lights Out nonetheless. Review-based product recommendations are a crucial application of sentiment analysis, 
where determining the pros and cons of a product greatly influences the user's preference. 
To improve the accuracy of recommendation, both the user's review content and the product's overall sentiment need to be taken into account. 
Despite the availability of sentiment-specific neural networks, most current approaches neglect the overall sentiment when predicting ratings or ranking products, 
while also overlooking how review content interacts with user features. 
To address these limitations, this paper proposes an interactive, sentiment-sensitive learning framework called SIFN, 
where a user's review content and overall sentiment are encoded and combined through an early interaction stage. 
Then, in the late interaction stage, product-specific features are combined with review-content and sentiment encodings. 
Notably, this model utilizes a overall sentiment encoder instead of simply utilizing a fixed sentiment label, 
allowing it to capture the complexity of user reviews. 
To support the interaction process, two attention mechanisms are built into SIFN, 
where the rating prediction stage is influenced by both review content and overall sentiment. 
As a result, this framework can effectively recommend products by considering user features, review content, and overall sentiment interdependencies. 
Testing on four datasets has validated the performance of SIFN and conducted thorough ablation studies to assess the impact of individual components. 
Furthermore, case studies have underscored the significance of distinguishing between positive and negative overall sentiments in review-based product recommendations. 
The source code and dataset are available at https://github.com/liujun-ksu/SIFN.

Using data augmentation to prepare training and evaluation sets is crucial for code-switched text classification, allowing models to handle variations in language mixing patterns. While numerous data augmentation techniques have been explored for monolingual and code-switched text, using Lexical Substitutions (LS) remains unexplored. We studied the effectiveness of an LS-based data augmentation method for the Arabic-English code-switched dataset CodeMix20. We evaluated different language modeling techniques, frequency-based word selection methods, and varying numbers of substitutions. Our results show that LS successfully generates high-quality mixes that are indistinguishable from the original data. Moreover, using LS data augmentation improved text classification performance on CodeMix20, with a 2% improvement in the best F1 score for a range of experimental configurations. We also introduced CodeMix20 with 2000 samples, a first in the field, aiding research in data augmentation and text classification. Our code will be freely accessible on GitHub.

Hexahedral mesh simplification is a highly valuable technique with numerous applications, primarily due to its ability to efficiently handle complex, detailed meshes. These detailed meshes contain a large number of tets compared to hexahedral volumes, making it necessary to find a balance between information loss and storage requirements. This research builds upon SimplifyHex, an advanced hexahedral mesh simplification algorithm, to further optimize it by reducing information loss through enhanced error estimation and refinement methods. The introduction of recursive mesh refinement enables the distribution of data from the original mesh to the simplified mesh, specifically onto tets with the shortest distance to hexahedral volumes. By combining error estimation and refinement, this updated algorithm can maintain accurate results even with a substantial number of tets, 58 percent of the original amount, while still offering significant data size reductions. The findings suggest that these details can be effectively allocated to tets with smaller amounts of extra volume, close to surface features or with simplified triangular representations. We introduce Coarse-Grained Continuity, a concept in reinforcement learning that builds upon the continuity concept in dynamic programming. This new idea leverages the structure of a Markov decision process to significantly reduce the high dimensionality typically associated with reinforcement learning. Specifically, we prove that in certain types of metric spaces, a key learning parameter has a continuous transition from one policy to another, when the change in action selection is gradually introduced. This theoretical finding leads to the development of multiple, more practical algorithms, each providing stronger guarantees based on the size of the state space, the reward values, and the transition probabilities. Our experimental results show that our algorithms perform equally well or better compared to existing methods. Given the computational challenges associated with verifying our continuity results, we also develop a verification algorithm, using a specialized tool, to test the Coarse-Grained Continuity of different policies across various examples. Our main contribution is the development of the Coarse-Grained Continuity concept, which reduces the complexity of the continuity problem in reinforcement learning, enabling the creation of multiple algorithms and methods. These findings pave the way for the development of more complex and high-performance reinforcement learning algorithms in the future. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation (CNS-1814100) and an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship. The code for our methods has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/krishnanr/CGC-RL. Our experiments used an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 graphics card. Our research was conducted at the University of Virginia. 

Key findings: 
- A general version of the Coarse-Grained Continuity concept was established for compact, metric spaces without isolated states.
- Our methods were extensively evaluated across 54 test cases, consisting of 36 basic test cases with detailed reward structures, as well as 18 more complex test cases modeling real-world scenarios.
- The empirical results demonstrated the effectiveness of the Coarse-Grained Continuity concept in reducing the complexity of the continuity problem in reinforcement learning. 
- Our methods were compared to existing reinforcement learning tools, with the results indicating that they perform equally well or better in practice. 
- A verification algorithm, using the Rtools tool, was employed to test the Coarse-Grained Continuity of different policies across various examples. 
- Future research could focus on the development of more complex and high-performance reinforcement learning algorithms. 
- Future work could involve the application of the Coarse-Grained Continuity concept to other domains and challenges.

In multi-agent learning systems, agents interact with each other through various behaviors such as movement, action, communication, etc. Some actions may be unsuccessful due to various reasons, but agents can try again by assessing the cause of failure and using this knowledge to modify their behavior. This process can be seen as an instance of intrinsic motivation, which encourages learning and adapts to environmental conditions. An important type of intrinsic motivation, transfer empowerment, improves performance by increasing agent autonomy. However, its dynamic nature, which requires adjustment as conditions change, is difficult to determine, especially in the presence of random failures. To address this limitation, a new approach called dependently re-responding transfer empowerment (DRTE) is introduced to overcome the challenge of establishing a lower bound on failure probability sampling distribution for non-iid scenarios. DRTE reformulates the learning paradigm as a minimax problem, which provides an optimal policy with the highest expected return under the current hypothesis for each step. By using Bayesian sampling to find the lower bound of the failure probability distribution, DRTE provides effective learning through both online and offline training methods and surpasses the performance of various state-of-the-art baselines in multiple testbeds. These testbeds include cooperative learning, which promotes the development of socially adaptive and dependably responsive behavior. Results show that DRTE outperforms all other baselines, which often fail to adapt to environmental changes by either overestimating their knowledge or neglecting the influence of random failures. Additionally, DRTE outperforms a successful cooperative learning approach called MCQ by 9.6% due to its inability to effectively learn under failure conditions. DRTE also performs better than a multi-agent transformer model tailored for social behavior by 13.6%, which can provide valuable insights into its behavioral analysis. Finally, DRTE outperforms a successful cooperative learning approach called novelty model by 14.6% despite its extensive training on failure conditions, which can provide valuable insights into its behavioral analysis. DRTE has the potential to be applied to a wide variety of multi-agent learning systems, which can be found in numerous real-world domains such as self-driving cars, social robots, etc. Furthermore, DRTE effectively promotes the development of socially adaptive and dependably responsive behavior by encouraging dependence on responsive partners and eliminating unnecessary exploration of unresponsive conditions. By utilizing a quantitative approach, we can establish a plan to correct and mitigate this bias. In this research, we present a method to accurately measure magnetic energy density in a unbiased way, which also serves as a model for addressing other common biases in solar data. By applying a unbiased conversion factor, we can adjust the existing solar magnetic field datasets, which also requires us to reassess many of the results from previous studies to ensure their accuracy and validity. Ultimately, we can achieve more reliable and accurate findings with the updated datasets. The process of acknowledging and mitigating this bias in VSFM data has important implications that extend beyond the conversion of flux densities to provide a stable foundation for future research. By applying a similar approach, we can also address other common biases in solar data. Von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem provides a robust estimate for the rate at which the average of measurable observations approaches their expected value. This paper offers a broader perspective on this theorem by examining the relationship between spectrum and convergence speed. It initially establishes methods for obtaining spectral distributions for non-stationary processes and provides a Frechet algebra framework for this purpose. By employing this approach, the paper derives bounds on the rate of convergence in von Neumann's Ergodent Theorem, both in its general and its ergodic form. These bounds are specifically demonstrated for Gaussian processes, where the problem of obtaining a spectral distribution is resolved through the use of two principles: the Stieltjes transformation, which characterizes the relationship between a measure and its cumulative function, and Choquet theory, which provides an alternative definition of a spectral measure as a representation of the spectrum of a differential operator. Several key results concerning the relationship between the scale of operators and the location of point masses on the spectrum are obtained, including a general theorem and two specialized theorems tailored to Hilbert and Frechet spaces. By employing these approaches, the paper derives a general bound on the rate of convergence in von Neumann's Ergodent Theorem of the form $O(\log^{-1}(T))$ for any $T\geq1$. Additionally, the paper obtains a more precise bound of the form $O(T^{-\frac{1}{4}}\log^{\frac{1}{2}}T)$. This work also examines an ergodic extension of this problem and its relation to almost periodic functions with short periods. By employing a Frechet space version of Bochner's theorem, the paper obtains a precise bound of the form $O(\log^{-\frac{7}{4}}T)$. Finally, the paper provides a general ergodicity criterion for sequences of operators in Frechet spaces and obtains a precise bound of the form $O(T^{-\epsilon}+\log^{-1}T)$. This work is concluded by obtaining a precise bound of the form $O(T^{-\frac{1}{2}}\log^{\frac{3}{2}}T)$ for Gaussian processes with the Banach norm. The techniques developed in this paper are also applied to a broader range of problems, including discrete systems, sequences of operators, and their ergodic extensions. The author also seeks, in a concluding chapter, to provide a simplified and comprehensive explanation of operator scale theory and the relationship between spectral measures and the distribution of eigenvalues

We have developed an effective method for identifying metal-poor stars in the early stages of a survey. By utilizing the broadband photometric data and spectra from the Gaia-ESO Public Survey, we employ machine learning techniques, specifically using decision tree and random forest algorithms, to classify stars based on their overall strength of magnesium lines and overall continuum flux. These stars were selected from the first public release of the Gaia-ESO Public Survey, which comprises 356 magnesium lines and broadband photometry from EPDCS fields. By utilizing the Gaia DR2 parallax, we are able to calculate the absolute magnitudes in various passbands and compare them to theoretical brightness limits. Additionally, we have derived essential demographic information for the selected sample, which includes key statistical parameters. We have compared our results to the selection process of the High Performance Survey, which utilizes distinct techniques for identifying metal-poor stars, and found our method to be both alternate and efficient. By applying these algorithms to select metal-poor stars, we have successfully chosen stars that are predominantly metal-poor, with the majority exhibiting very low metal content. Following further observations using low-resolution spectroscopy, the selected samples have been refined to include approximately 90% metal-poor stars at the $T_{\rm{eff}}$ ranges necessary for future studies. These selected samples now cover a broader temperature range of $4500 < T_{\rm{eff}} < 6000$K and include metal-poor stars up to a distance of 1 kpc. By utilizing these selected samples, we have created two new databases, which include metal-poor stars with low Reid metallicity definition and those with Reid definition. Deep neural networks are often deployed in environments requiring limited resources, such as restricted CPU power, limited memory, or slow network connections. Large, trained models cannot be transferred due to the high cost of storage and transmission. Therefore, a compressed model with reduced size and adaptability to limited resource environments is desired. A common method for model compression involves representing a neural network as a set of quantized weights and embedded layers. However, this approach is not suitable for limited resource environments as it demands significant processing power and memory. In such environments, we propose introducing a level of abstraction by observing only a subset of the data and its effects on the network during training. The network learns to predict the unobserved data, resulting in a compact model that generalizes well to the unobserved data. Our method focuses on selecting and processing crucial data features, giving rise to novel model compression strategies. By applying this idea to an ensemble of models, we developed a novel compression strategy for unsupervised settings. Our proposed approach is universally applicable to top-down model compression methods. Our empirical evaluation on various datasets and with different architectures shows that it surpasses existing methods in terms of compression ratio while maintaining or improving accuracy. Additionally, the idea is validated through its analytical generalization properties. By making the PyTorch code available, the code (https://github.com/alexk43/partial-obs) can be accessed. Firstly, we identify key distinctions between the underlying structural properties that enable their maintenance. Although QKD is considered a secure method of obtaining secret keys, it does not offer protection against data privacy attacks. To address this limitation, an attack-resistant source of privacy enhancement is introduced in this research. This improved source uses a non-uniform random model based on real-world data to evaluate bound values for QKD systems, providing a more accurate assessment of secret key generation capabilities. Two main attacks, collective and individual attacks, are considered, and corresponding source strength and secrecy factors are derived from optimal measurement strategies defined by positive operator-valued measures. Numerical calculations demonstrate the impact of non-uniform randomness on QKD key generation, highlighting reduced vulnerability to collective attacks but increased reduction in secrecy for individual attacks. Furthermore, source bound values and secret key generation capacities are examined in practical QKD systems, showcasing the influence of non-uniform randomness on real-world distances and secret key generation. Finally, source bound values and secret key generation capacities are graphically presented for comparison with uniform randomness. This study serves as a practical guide for evaluating QKD system performance with non-uniform random sources, supporting effective deployment in various real-world scenarios. Additionally, source bound values and secret key generation capacities are provided in tabular form for comparison with uniform randomness. The research offers valuable insights into non-uniform random source impact on QKD systems, facilitating effective evaluation and comparison with uniform randomness. The study's findings are presented in a comprehensive and detailed manner.

This work centers on a boosted dark energy model with spin-dependent diffusion, where the dark energy particle is initially in a state of pure spin. We apply the WKB method to examine the effective potential seen by the spin-dependent particle, taking into account various values of $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$. Consequently, we analyze the behavior of the particle's orbits, its turning points, and the consequential values of the effective potential at the points of turn around. Furthermore, we calculate the particle's density distribution within a Schwarzschild black hole and its associated radial probability density, ultimately yielding the shape parameters $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ of the distribution for diverse values of the effective potential, $\epsilon$, and $\lambda$. The study then evaluates the classical mobility of the dark matter in a Schwarzschild black hole, where we compute the diffusion coefficient and define the normalized velocity of the diffusion, ultimately examining the effects of the parameters $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ on the velocity of diffusion. The research then explores the spin-dependent energy model in a model of a charged Schwarzschild black hole, where we compute the radial probability density and the shape parameters $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ for diverse values of the parameters $\epsilon$, $\lambda$, and the charge of the black hole, $q$. Given that $c_n$ can also be expressed as $c_n = 4 \int_0^1 x^n (1-x)^n dx$, this relation provides a new insight into the polynomial approximation of functions. $\text{sign}(P_n(x)-P_{n-1}(x))=\ldots =\text{sign}(P_1(x)-P_0(x))=-1.$
This result holds for all positive even n and any polynomials $P_{n-1}(x),\ldots,P_0(x)$ with real coefficients. Continuous-phase modulation (CPM) is noted for its straightforward signal structure and simple demodulation processes, along with a combination of robustness and spectral efficiency. Non-coherent detection of CPM can be accomplished with a time delay of no more than 2L^2, where L represents the number of symbols within a symbol phrase length. This delay can be less than 2L^2 for certain types of CPM with rotational symmetry, such as rotating CPM. Nevertheless, even with reduced delay times, non-coherent detection still demands significant computational resources due to the need for expensive signal correlation. In contrast, this research demonstrates that a basic CPM system based on traditional components can perform non-coherent detection in as few clock cycles as 4L^2, resulting in substantial improvements through this simplified approach. This paper presents the derivation of the CPM detection algorithm, an examination of its asymptotic behavior, and a comparison with alternative methods. Moreover, we showcase that this simplified design can also be applied to state-of-the-art CPM variants, featuring significant energy efficiency gains. This new process further reduces to 4L^2 clock cycles for certain types of CPM with rotational symmetry. This simplified CPM detection has the added benefit of being compatible with existing CPM protocols, making it possible to perform CPM-based communications in as few clock cycles as 4L^2. This approach is then further adapted for CPM systems with hash functions, where it results in highly secure yet resource-efficient CPM-based communications that can perform around 40 million operations per second while using less than 0.5 MB of RAM. Ultimately, we show that this simplified design can be utilized for both secure CPM-based protocols and efficient CPM data storage, allowing for fast storage of CPM-based data. This agent-based data can be misleading, as it often prioritizes skills over rewarding behaviors. To resolve this limitation, our Visually Aided Reward Learning method employs a novel cluster ranking technique that combines visual features and reward properties to guide the learning process. This approach prioritizes sample ranking over traditional agent data over time, yielding a more efficient and consistent reward function. Furthermore, our method integrates with reinforcement learning and showcases exceptional results on classic games, outperforming existing visually aided reward learning methods. As data-driven decision-making gains prominence within our lives and workplaces, the need to analyze and understand the internal workings of algorithms grows.  Despite numerous approaches to measuring interpretability, the concept remains poorly defined, hindering its applicability in practical settings.  In this paper, I suggest a new, theoretically grounded approach to understanding and assessing algorithmic interpretability by considering a learning process involving a human observer.  By combining cognitive psychology principles, the complexity of both the learning process and the algorithm itself can be quantified.  This new approach, known as the Cognitive Intricacy Score (CIS), is tested on a range of supervised learning algorithms covering various categories.  By evaluating CIS in comparison to existing metrics, the study reveals that human learning is influenced more by an algorithm's logical structure than its performance and the clarity of its output, thus the CIS better reflects the interpretability of algorithms that involve logical complexity, such as decision trees.  On the other hand, algorithms lacking logical structure, such as neural networks and support vector machines, appear more difficult to understand from a human perspective, despite their ease of operation.  Furthermore, CIS analysis highlights the interpretability of algorithms used less frequently or in specific domains as lower than average, suggesting a need to develop more straightforward versions of these algorithms to improve their understanding among human learners.  This study proposes a new, theoretically grounded assessment framework and a quantifiable method, CIS, to measure the interpretability of algorithms from a human learning perspective, thus providing both theoretical and practical insights that can guide the development of more understandable algorithms.  In addition to these findings, several potential applications of CIS are also discussed.  In summary, the main contributions of this paper are threefold.  Firstly, a new, theoretically grounded approach to understanding and assessing algorithmic interpretability by considering a human learning process is introduced.  Secondly, a quantifiable method, CIS, to measure the interpretability of algorithms from a human learning perspective is developed and tested.  Finally, several potential applications of CIS to various areas such as algorithmic development, education and the evaluation of future algorithms are explored.  Future research could focus on developing a systematic and comprehensive CIS measurement framework and applying it to a broader range of algorithms and contexts. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed for analyzing extreme events' occurrence frequencies with time-to-event data following a non-stationary, climate-driven pattern. Extreme events can often be modeled by a Poisson process, and such modeling offers flexibility in relating event frequencies to climate variables, while also accounting for potential correlations in time. A parameterization for non-stationary Poisson processes has been introduced that allows for a coordinated examination of extreme events' changing intensity and periodicity in relation to climate data. An explicit Bayesian framework has been created for this new parameterization using Gaussian autoregressive models for time-varying components. This method has several beneficial characteristics: it places posterior constraints on future event probabilities, calculates quantile-based return levels that correlate with climate data, and enables regularization of estimation based on extrapolated data. The proposed method's effectiveness has been supported through theoretical simulations and real-world data analysis, specifically from oceanic regime shifts and extreme floods in El Ni\~no conditions. The latter case's findings include a link between sea surface height (SSH) and flood frequency, and a prediction that SSH trends could substantially increase future flood risk. The method's code is accessible via the R package extremegeo, which includes pre-installed functionality for climate-driven extrapolation of extreme events. 

Please note that this work was originally published in https://arXiv.org/ and the related code can be found in https://cran.r-project.org/. 

Related key-words: Bayesian inference, climate change, extreme events, Poisson process, time-to-event data.

This work examines the behavior of cross-sectional areas in junctions formed by two linear roads, focusing on their stationary points. We identify both the conditions necessary for these stationary points and their precise geometric locations. Additionally, we analyze the average cross-sectional area of these junctions under different conditions and find the areas where this average remains stationary. Our study demonstrates that there are both local and global stationary points, and we provide the specific geometric configurations in which they occur. Moreover, we investigate the relationships between these stationary points and the x-fold convexity property, which arises when the average cross-sectional area has a stationary value for the first time. The property is shown to be dependent on the junction geometry, specifically on the angles and lengths of the overlapping road sections. The number of folds, x, is determined by these geometric settings, and we precisely define the areas in which each x-fold occurrence takes place. We also discuss how (x,n)-convexity, where (x,n) is a tuple consisting of the number of folds and junction sites, affects the problem and consider the possibility of extending our findings to more complex road systems. The results of this study could be useful in designing optimal road networks by identifying the areas with stationary average cross-sectional areas. Furthermore, we relate these results to a theoretical model of biological growth, showing that the properties of a one-dimensional growth model can be applied to road junctions, even those with multiple road sections. We precisely define the conditions necessary for the growth model's stationary points and identify the specific geometric settings in which they occur. We also derive the (1,3)-convexity equation for the growth model, which is shown to be related to the third moment of the binary function. The model's stationary points are further analyzed by considering a sequence of junctions with increasing stationary points, which converges to a limiting junction. We investigate the properties of this sequence and its relationship to the (x,n)-convexity property. Specifically, we show that the (1,n+1)-convexity property is equivalent to the limit of the sequence's (x,n)-convexity property as x tends to infinity. Moreover, we precisely determine the birth-and-growth sequence's properties and the conditions necessary for its convergence to a square. These experiments demonstrate that FGNET-RH outperforms contemporary methods in terms of accuracy on entity classification tasks. In recent years, the internal workings of datacenter management have been increasingly scrutinized. Certain datacenter management strategies, such as load balancing and virtual machine reservation, have garnered significant attention. This research focuses on the challenge of reserved VMs request arrival and dynamic workloads' load distribution in datacenters. Our proposed solution, Prepartition, addresses the limitations of existing boundary partition (BP) method by mitigating its primary shortcomings: inaccurate prediction of reserved requests and boundary blurring. Prepartition employs user's reserved requests and future non-reserved workload observations to define partition points within the reserved regions, thereby achieving more precise load distribution. Our theoretical model, experimental evaluation, and real-world assessment demonstrate Prepartition's performance superiority over boundary partition, notably under reserved requests uncertainty and boundary blurring conditions. Based on our findings, Prepartition offers approximately 15% higher quality of service (QoS) performance in scenarios with 50% reserved requests and boundary blurring, compared to boundary partition. Furthermore, Prepartition outperforms boundary partition by 40-100% in real-world cloud scenarios. Our comprehensive evaluation of Prepartition highlights its potential as a load distribution strategy capable of addressing reserved VMs request arrival and dynamic workloads in datacenters. The movement of stars can be influenced by the presence of unseen companions. This study examines the potential properties of these hidden companions and their impact on the movement of five nearby accelerated stars. Utilizing the SARH code, we analyzed low-resolution spectra from the Hectospec instrument to derive precise velocity measurements for these stars. Subsequently, we calculated the masses and orbital distances of hypothetical companions, assuming circular and edge-on orbits. Our results indicate that the parameters of accelerated stars G164-12, G208-12, and G251-12 cannot be precisely determined due to limited resolution, whereas non-accelerated stars HD 5058 and HD 80667 can have their properties accurately estimated. A widely employed modulation technique, Gray-coded cooperative multiple access, uses distinct phase shifts for separate user data streams. However, its encoding process is complicated and energy inefficient due to requiring accurate computation of phase shift values. A simplified yet efficient solution to this problem can be found in binary amplitude phase shift keying, which encodes the phase shift values directly into binary and applies a fixed decoding strategy. Our research aims to develop a cooperative multiple access scheme that combines the benefits of GCMA and BAPSK. We introduced a new quantization method, which uses a neural network to minimize the error between desired and obtained phase shift estimates. Our experiments showed that this approach significantly outperforms existing quantization methods in terms of overall system performance. We found that the optimal quantization threshold varies depending on channel conditions and that the network can self-adjust to achieve the best performance under different channel scenarios. Notably, our results indicate that the neural network can effectively eliminate the noise in phase shift estimates without affecting data accuracy, which allows for reduced quantization bits when the noise effect is minimal. A complementary network can be used to determine the optimal quantization threshold by analyzing the noise effect on the neural quantization results, which in turn leads to lower error rates when the neural quantization output is used. Our experiments showed that the use of these two networks results in a significant improvement in overall system performance compared to the use of a single network, which adds support for the feasibility of a BAPSK-based cooperative multiple access scheme that combines the benefits of GCMA and BAPSK. Our findings open up the possibility for future research to incorporate more complex postprocessing methods after deep learning-based quantization to further improve system performance. Notably, our results were obtained through simulations using fewer than 2000 samples per channel curve, which allows for the generalization of our findings to real-world channel scenarios. Furthermore, our approach can be easily adapted for the design of other modulation techniques, which at the moment does not exist in literature yet. Importantly, our research showcases the significance of a BAPSK-based cooperative multiple access scheme that combines the benefits of GCMA and BAPSK, which at the moment does not exist in literature yet. This paper presents SSCAP, a novel approach for unsupervised segmental action detection based on a deep neural network model. SSCAP starts with a two-stream convolutional neural network that processes video frames and their temporal derivatives, allowing it to capture both action appearances and temporal evolution through low-level feature aggregation. Current action detection approaches heavily depend on strong and costly supervision to identify the main actor(s) involved in actions. To overcome this limitation, this work presents an novel framework that utilizes sparse and easily obtainable labelling, specifically instance-centred scene annotations. Each person in a scene is labelled as either an 'actor', but the specific action they perform is not specified, making these annotations weakly-guided. The goal is to automatically extract the relevant instance information necessary for action detection. To achieve this, we introduce a new network called GCN4AD, which integrates graph convolutional networks to capture the spatial and temporal context of actors, allowing it to accurately determine the actions performed. The model's effectiveness was tested on benchmarks like 20Salience and ActivityNet, where it outperforms or matches state-of-the-art action detection approaches while requiring fewer labels. Additionally, we introduce an new dataset called SAL-CROWD, which replicates salience-based evaluation metrics using the crowded dataset ACDC. The Image Clef challenge in Out-of-Context Recognition, also known as Image Similarity (IS), took place for the second time in 2021 with a modified track that didn't involve human ratings. Instead of rating similarity, the task focused on identifying the most relevant images, which allowed for a broader range of submissions than before. 

There were four datasets used in the challenge, each with its unique characteristics: a set of concert photos with a diverse range of topics, images of food with varying degrees of relevance, a set of product photos with clear categories and a set of travel images with geographical connections. 

A total of 32 participants joined the challenge, with 28 teams competing in the ranking track and 16 teams competing in the retrieval track. 

The challenge's results showed that teams excelled at identifying image similarity when using retrieval methods but struggled with ranking when the similarity range varied. 

A key finding of the challenge was that human evaluations and machine ratings aligned in terms of the most highly rated images but diverged for less highly rated images. 

The challenge's complete results and all the submitted data, including code and models, have been made available online for the public.

Document analysis, specifically for tables, becomes increasingly complex when dealing with documents of high information density and nuanced structure. As tables grow to contain more cells, featuring varied layouts and contents, the task of accurately identifying and interpreting them within documents becomes a challenging and error-prone endeavor, especially when accompanied by poor quality scans and font rendering issues. One technique that shows promise in addressing these complexities is the use of Graph Neural Networks, as tables can be effectively represented as connected graph structures, facilitating analysis and interpretation by an neural network. However, the success of this approach relies on the accurate extraction and encoding of table information, a task made difficult by the presence of noisy input and tables with intricate structures. This study investigates the impact of diverse table encodings on the performance of Graph Neural Networks and proposes a method of automatically determining the most effective representation through an analysis of the table's structure. Our research demonstrates that tailored encodings outperform generic methods, while also revealing that a specific graph structure and attention-based graph neural network are the key components required to achieve excellence in table extraction tasks. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that automatically selecting the most effective representation results in superior extraction performance when compared to using a single standard encoding. By exploring the impact of diverse encodings, we are able to propose automatic table encoding and graph structure selection methods that enable a significant improvement in performance, ultimately leading to the achievement of an impressive 99.8% accuracy for table extraction. This achievement serves as a major milestone in this field of study. The proposed methodology and associated code have been made publicly available. As a result, our research aims to stimulate further advancements in this area. The primary contribution of our work lies in the area of table encodings, as we seek to promote a deeper comprehension of the diverse table encodings that could be created and their effect on the performance of machine learning models. Moreover, our research contributes to the field of self-adjusting machine learning systems by proposing a method of automatically selecting the most effective table encoding from a variety of possibilities. The final area of contribution lies in the area of graph structures, as we seek to promote a deeper comprehension of the diverse graph structures that could be applied to tables and their effect on the performance of machine neural networks. utilizing these devices to speed up the training and inference processes of
neural networks. Certain techniques such as data filtering can take advantage
of edge devices' computational capabilities, enabling more efficient data
processing on lower bandwidth devices like IoT sensors. A proposed method,
the Membership Query Filter, can filter data on edge devices without needing
to transfer the original data, by using model queries to identify relevant
information. However, this technique still requires a part of the data to be
transferred to build the query filter. To address this limitation, we introduced
a False Positive Free Collection method, enabling the creation of query filters
without any error for collections of data without any false positives, by
selecting samples that include at least one false negative. This innovation
eliminates the need for transferring any data, as only selected samples are
transferred. We provide a mathematical analysis of our approach and test its
efficiency through experiments using convolutional neural networks for different
classification tasks. Overall, this technique enables the creation of false
positive free collections with various models and datasets, and significantly

Effective training of machine learning models is crucial for superconducting quantum processors, where unique error correction techniques must be applied. Unmonitored learning occurs naturally during the self-healing process of these devices, while instructed learning involves adjusting the weight of model parameters based on specific data analysis. The complexity of superconducting quantum processors presents significant computational challenges, rendering traditional simulation methods impractical. Therefore, simplifying these simulations is essential to enable their consideration in larger-scale research. We have developed a simplified simulation method for both unmonitored and instructed learning on these devices, which is applicable for up to 5 qubit systems. Additionally, simulations for up to 23 qubit systems are performed without full detail, confirming that instructed learning can improve data processing quality, although for superconducting quantum processors, unmonitored learning appears to be more effective under equal training time. However, further research is needed to explore the potential of instructed learning in enhancing data processing capabilities. The simulations conducted without full detail suggest that unmonitored learning could achieve 93% accuracy with 23 qubits, whereas instructed learning could reach 90% accuracy. We have also determined the optimal qubit distribution for the qubit-based classifier, finding that equally sized clusters yield the highest accuracy (93% for 23 qubits and 91% for 21 qubits). The ability to perform spatiottemporal reasoning is a crucial component of humans and artificial intelligence systems, which involves making precise judgments about points in time and space. To develop advanced AI capable of real-world applications such as project management and image processing, it's essential to create efficient models for reasoning about spatial and temporal information. Recent studies have introduced graph-based models for improving spatiotemporal reasoning, which have shown significant gains in performance. Building upon this foundation, we introduce the Hopper model, a multi-hop approach for precise spatiotemporal reasoning that surpasses current standards. The model's architecture enables it to jump between interconnected entities, which are represented by nodes in the graph, allowing for precise judgments to be made. By leveraging knowledge graphs, the Hopper model can learn to connect entities and make accurate predictions by recognizing relationships between them. Experimental results demonstrate that the Hopper model achieves remarkable results on the LEO dataset, which is particularly challenging due to its complexity. Notably, the model performs exceptionally well even on more intricate queries that require a deep understanding of the spatial and temporal relationships between entities. Additionally, the model's efficiency has been accurately reflected in its computational time, which is measured in terms of the number of hops it takes to reach the answer. Furthermore, we present a novel explanation for the Hopper model's performance by analyzing its ability to navigate through the spatial and temporal relationships between entities. The model's ability to hop between interconnected entities reveals complex patterns and groupings that are not immediately apparent from the entity distribution, which explains its performance on different types of queries. Ultimately, the analysis demonstrates that the Hopper model's success is rooted in its ability to recognize entity patterns and groupings that correspond to real-world complexities, which is an essential aspect of precise spatiotemporal reasoning. The analysis can be found in the companion paper. The code for the Hopper model is available at https://github.com/krux95/Hopper. The traditional Bayesian hierarchical linear model, consisting of a primary model and two subordinate models representing group-level and individual-level factors, has a more predictable and orderly structure. Similar to standard Bayesian models, where prior distributions inform parameters, making them more predictable, this model works the same way. Its first step involves specifying distribution types for slower and more unpredictable variance components, followed by calculating the parameters of the prior distributions in the second step by using available data. By employing Bayesian techniques such as Markov chain Monte Carlo, the parameters of the prior distributions can be estimated when only a limited amount of information is available about group- and individual-level factors. Consequently, the estimated models function as the prior distributions' parameters, allowing researchers to use the available data. In the third step, the estimated models are applied to new, entirely new data. Given its clear and logical structure, the BHLM is an easily interpretable method for estimating group- and individual-level factors when there is a limited amount of information. Furthermore, the theoretical foundations of the approach provide a clear justification for making inferences about group-level factors when there is a limited amount of information. A step-by-step guide to implementing a basic Bayesian hierarchical linear model using R is provided as an example. The example data comes from a study by Kovasich (1988)[31], which looked at the effect of education on earnings in different states. The findings illustrate the effectiveness of the approach in estimating the effect of education on earnings at the state and individual levels. In the end, some potential areas for expansion and improvement of the approach are discussed.

The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model has been widely used for adaptive function approximation and has extensive applications in various fields. However, its traditional version encounters a deadlock during training, leading to a failure in descending the loss function. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a unified family of closed-form unbiased score matching estimators, which consistently outperform the traditional maximum-likelihood-based estimator in both speed and convergence rate. Furthermore, our estimator can be efficiently updated using stochastic gradient descent, enabling a dramatic reduction in training complexity from $O(L^2)$ to $O(L)$. Our unbiased estimator also eliminates the need for a balance regularization technique, thus providing more freedom in model design and evaluation. We validate the performance of our estimator in MoE architecture through theoretical analysis, empirical experiments, and real-world applications, especially in light of our recently established convergence results for training MoE. We also provide a comprehensive comparison with the traditional balance-based MoE model on a variety of tasks, demonstrating that our estimator achieves significant improvements in model quality, training speed, and convergence rate. Lastly, we highlight the unique capabilities of our estimator, including its ability to handle high-dimensional tasks, a challenging task for traditional balance-based MoE models. Our corresponding code can be found at https://github.com/ChenDongDong/ScoreMatchForMoE. Additionally, our pre-trained MoE models, developed on large-scale benchmark datasets, are hosted on https://github.com/ChenDongDong/Pre-Trained-Model-For-MoE. These resources are intended to facilitate the advancement of MoE research and the development of related applications. To address potential concerns regarding the deadlocks in our updated training process, we have revised the code and the corresponding console output for reproducibility purposes, available at https://github.com/ChenDongDong/Score-Match-For-MoE-Reproduce. Our contributions have been thoroughly reviewed and verified to guarantee the accuracy and validity of our work. The relevant proof of our contributions can be found at https://github.com/ChenDongDong/Score-Match-For-MoE-Reprove. Our work has been thoroughly reviewed and verified by experts, as documented in the review process, available at https://github.com/ChenDongDong/Score-Match-For-MoE-Review. We investigate the generation of magnetic fields at the Grand Unified Theory (GUT) and Planck scales by investigating the violation of Lorentz symmetry in quantum gravity, which leads to distinct possibilities: kinematical violations occurring at a specific, low temperature scale apart from other scales; dynamical violations occurring at the Planck or GUT scales; and anomalous violations occurring at various, unrelated scales. To examine the dynamics of quantum gravity, we evaluate the possibility that phase transitions create magnetic fields through QCD and electroweak forces, but the gap between GUT and the Grand Unified Theory scales is too narrow for this to occur effectively. This leaves us to analyze the possibility of magnetic fields created at the Planck scale by backreaction from quantum gravity, which is associated with the dynamical violations. To investigate this, we evaluate the possibility that such a phase transition occurs at the GUT scale, which would result in detectable, large-scale birefringence of light, measurable by BELLSC and DECIGO experiments. Conversely, our analysis of the kinematical violations, occurring at low temperatures or in laboratory experiments, does not preclude the possibility that such a scale remains high, up to the GUT scale. Finally, our discussion of the anomalies, occurring at various, unrelated scales, is necessarily limited to the possibility that such a scale may exist above the GUT scale, as such deviations occurring below this scale are unable to generate magnetic fields through QCD and electroweck forces. Overall, our findings indicate that if the gap between the Planck and GUT scales remains large, then the dynamical violations offer the most likely possibility, while the kinematical and anomalous violations respectively remain less and less likely. In any case, our analysis stresses that the dynamics of quantum gravity likely play a critical role in the early universe. Furthermore, our findings indicate that any scale at which the kinematical violations occur must not exceed the GUT scale. Lastly, our discussion reveals that any anomalies occurring at lower scales than the kinematical ones do not preclude the possibility that such a scale may exist above the GUT scale, as such deviations occurring above this scale can generate magnetic fields through QCD and electroweak forces more effectively. Thus our analysis has implications beyond quantum gravity, also influencing electroweak theory. Furthermore, our findings have significant implications beyond theoretical considerations, also influencing experimental and astrophysical investigations. In particular, our discussion has significant implications for future research into BELLSC and DECIGO

In various scenarios, such as biological and social systems, global phenomena often stem from interactions between numerous local entities. Human migration, the spread of diseases, and financial transactions exemplify information dissemination processes that are crucial for the functioning and development of complex networks. Notably, the speed at which this information is disseminated significantly impacts the overall system operation and structure. In this work, we aim to investigate how network topology affects the efficiency of information dissemination. Employing a straightforward model where nodes are activated at random times and communicate locally, we demonstrate that a phase transition is possible in this process, where the speed of information dissemination may be either finite or infinite. Through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulation, we reveal that this speed is influenced by a dimensionless parameter capturing the quantifiable division of the network into distinct components. Ultimately, our results suggest that a moderately divided network optimally facilitates the rapid dissemination of global information. Nonetheless, the optimal division degree might vary depending on specific systems under consideration and the nature of the information being transmitted. Furthermore, our model and findings could potentially be applied to a wide range of systems, such as fundamental physics and biology, as well as social and economic environments. Given its simplicity, this model could serve as a versatile tool for examining various aspects of information propagation. Furthermore, our results show that a network can be represented as being composed of either distinct communities or uniform entities, depending on the parameter value, denoting a form of network phase transition. Consequently, the division degree of a network might hold significance in understanding its structure and the mechanisms underlying its information dissemination. To further explore this concept, we conducted additional numerical simulations by considering a few hypothetical scenarios. Ultimately, our research suggests that a network division degree of roughly one can lead to the most efficient information dissemination. Given the general simplicity of our model and the wide range of applications to which it could potentially be applied, the notion of network division degree deserves more attention and further investigation. As an example, we considered a system comprising two types of nodes, where the majority communicate locally, but some nodes are capable of long-distance communication. Specifically, we will show that as the size of the model increases, the advantage provided by additional parameters diminishes, leading to a scenario where extremely overparameterized networks may struggle to generalize even on smaller scales.
