We evaluate the transmission distance of dual-polarization 4D formats, considering both IMP and DIF nonlinear distortion types. We develop an approximate formula for the IMP distance, building on existing work by Kovalev et al, and test it against direct simulations. The analysis also reveals a counterintuitive result: the incorporation of spatial diversity in dual-polarization systems can actually increase the susceptibility to nonlinear distortion. We conduct a comprehensive comparison of the performance of two 4D formats, revealing that the selection of linearly polarized subcarriers has a considerable impact on the system's distance capabilities. Finally, we investigate the 4D format's ability to achieve ideal capacity when subjected to differential nonlinearity, revealing a notable connection between its design and the required nonlinear distortion power. This research sheds light on the design principles of dual-polarization 4D formats, aiding in the creation of systems capable of withstanding significant nonlinear distortion over long distances. Notably, the analysis indicates that the potential reach of WDM 4D transmission is significantly greater than in traditional two-polarization systems, with reaches exceeding 1 300 km and 2 000 km for the M-4D-A1 and M-4D-A3 formats under standard nonlinear conditions. By operating at a low code rate of 1.1, the maximum possible distance of M-4D-A3 is theoretically over 3 500 km, albeit requiring an extremely low disturbance power of around 0.2 W^-1.metro^-2. Consequently, the presented findings are viewed as a crucial starting point for the design of dual-polarization 4D transmission systems. Analysis of their potential extensions beyond the limits of conventional nonlinear models indicates that the maximum possible reach of dual-polarization systems could be as much as 3 500 km, thereby transforming them into a highly efficient solution for the line and the metro. Importantly, the presented designs hold considerable value for systems incorporating new types of nonlinear distortion mitigation methods. Moreover, the M-4D-A3 format offers a high degree of potential for coexistence with FBG-based channels in FBG networks. Ultimately, the presented research is viewed as a highly valuable discovery that unlocks the full potential of 4D formats as an efficient solution for various applications. Notably, the presented findings are expected to significantly influence the design of future dual-polarization 4D format systems. Moreover, the presented models and formulas can serve as essential tools for designers working on 4D format systems

In a recommender system, users' intentions play a crucial role. However, current approaches often focus solely on short-term goals, overlooking the complex underlying motivations. Determining user motivations in real-time is impractical due to their diverse nature. To address this, we focus on uncovering a user's hidden motivation for sequences of items, which can enhance both motivation modeling and recommendation generation. To tackle this challenge, we employ a dual HMM model that models both the user's short-term goals and long-term motivations. By using a large dataset of movie ratings, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in uncovering user motivations. Notably, our results indicate that users are often motivated by a mix of factors, rather than a singular one. Building on this model, we develop a novel recommendation algorithm that utilizes both short-term and long-term recommendations. To tackle the issue of model parameter inflation, we employ a hierarchical approach that shares parameters across overlapping subgroups of users. The experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves significantly better performance compared to a baseline motivation model and the standard item-based recommendation approach. The source code is publicly available on GitHub.

The classification of a specific type of linear differential equations, known as transformable double confluent Heun equations, is investigated in two parts. Firstly, we identify all generalized Fuchsian fuchsiant points for these equations. Secondly, we apply a general method to obtain a specialization of the equations, which has the effect of removing all irregularity from the original differential equation. This process yields a set of distinct ordinary differential equations, each corresponding to a unique fuchsiant point. Furthermore, we provide a criterion for determining if two fuchsiant points can be combined into a single, folded point, as well as a way to calculate the monodromy matrix for the unfolded differential equation. Additionally, we consider a specific model unfolding method and explain its implications on the monodromy of the original differential equation. The results we obtain are general and apply to a wide range of linear differential equations, including those classified in \cite{thomas2013families}. The key idea behind our findings relies on the fact that the monodromy of a Fuchsian differential equation is determined by a single ordinary differential equation corresponding to a generalized fuchsiant point. This idea extends to hyperholomorphic equations, where we define a similar notion of source based on a four-dimensional singular manifold with four distinct points. The monodromy of a hyperholomorphic equation is determined by a similar type of model unfolding, where we consider a four-dimensional hyperholomorphic unfolding of the source over the parameter space. The model hyperholomorphic unfoldings provide a general framework for investigating the Birkhoff fibration in the context of a holomorphic vector bundle. The results we obtain are particularly relevant for the holomorphic 2d Yang-Mills equations, where we consider a generalized Fuchsian singularity in the second spin component. When this singularity is folded into the zero section of the second spin bundle, the resulting ordinary differential equation determines the monodromy of the original differential equation. This study investigates the rank-one matrix approximation problem with group-wise heterogeneity. In this context, we group matrix entries into various sets, applying different penalty matrices to these groups in matrix approximation. A thorough investigation of this problem yields several key findings. First, we identify the tightness of the optimality conditions for this problem, drawing essential ideas from the rank-one matrix approximation without group-wise heterogeneity. Additionally, we explore the existence and location of these essential limits. Our analysis also highlights the distinct optimization characteristics that arise from the interaction of multiple penalty matrices, illustrating how they influence the set of essential matrices. Furthermore, we establish criteria to gauge the "closeness" of these essential limits and demonstrate that these criteria are adaptable to various matrix approximation scenarios. Lastly, we illustrate the relevance of these findings to practical applications by using numerical methods to investigate the relationship between US death rates and underlying factors. The semi-inclusive version of the lepton flavor universality ratio $R_{K/\Gamma_2}$ is proposed to test the effects of missing high-frequency vector and axial-vector currents in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions. By analyzing a single observable, the double differential rate $d\Gamma_{K\to\pi\nu\bar{\nu}}/dq^2$, is decomposed into two parts: a fully inclusive rate and a semi-inclusive rate, allowing a direct test of local lepton flavor universality without unitarity constraints. Assuming no additional new physics sources, the semi-inclusive rate is determined to be $R_{K/\Gamma_2}^{SM}=1.0004$ with minimal sensitivity to $|V_{cb}|$. If new physics is present, it can be detected at a $1\sigma$ confidence level for a $3\sigma$ deviation in $R_{K}$ and $q^2$-averaged $R_{K^{(*)}}$. A search for new physics can be interpreted in terms of Wilson coefficients, and specific constraints on $C_{P,S'}$ and $C'_{9,10}$ can be derived. The proposed test has favorable outlooks, such as being sensitive to $\text{TeV}^{-1}$ new physics energy scales with the Belle II experiment, and can also be performed with the Belle II and future Belle-II phase-2 and LHCb experiments. When working with incomplete data sets, it is usual to analyze the data's non-response rate. In some cases, this non-response might be predictive of the data missing entirely, making analysis challenging. In this scenario, analysis of the data's non-ignorably missing, given key variables known as predictors, can be complicated. Ignorably missing data can be analyzed using standard methods, but non-ignorably missing data requires application of specialized techniques. One such technique is the e-value introduced by Wakefield (2016), which estimates how strongly a predictor affects missing data given additional information. The e-value offers numerous benefits over traditional measures like odds ratios. Specifically, it avoids issues related to confounding variables and missing data, making it a robust option. To better understand the e-value's performance, a simulation study analyzing the e-value and related measures was conducted. Results indicate that the e-value offers more accurate insights into the data's non-response rate than other methods. Furthermore, a real-world example involving data on patients using Naloxone to reverse opioid overdoses has been included to demonstrate the practical application of the e-value in Bayesian missing data analysis. 

Keywords: Bayesian inference, missing data, non-ignorably missing data, sensitivity analysis, E-value.

The study of charm and beauty hadrons at the LHCb experiment involves analyzing the production of non-prompt and prompt D0 and D+ mesons in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV center-of-mass energy. This research focuses on the transverse momentum and rapidity distributions of non-prompt D mesons, as well as beauty-quark tagging. It is the first measurement of non-prompt D0 and D+ meson production in proton-proton collisions at a specified energy. To achieve these measurements, data from three integrated luminosities of 0.37, 0.36, and 2.0 fb$^{-1}$ were collected during 2015, 2016, and 2015, respectively, and experimental findings were corrected for detector efficiency, mis-identification, and other factors. Subsequent analysis revealed that non-prompt D0 meson production at the rapidity of 2.5 and transverse momentum of 4.0 GeV exhibits the lowest beauty-elegance ratio among all measured conditions, while D+ meson production at the rapidity of 2.3 and transverse momentum of 6.5 GeV displays the highest ratio. Moreover, within the measured ranges, both prompt and non-prompt D0 and D+ meson production at the LHCb experiment exhibit linearity when compared to similar past studies at the Tevatron and RHIC experiments. We are now leveraging this platform to test the thermal management strategies of quantum computers incorporating multiple resonators. Many robotic systems face challenges in navigating unfamiliar urban settings
due to a lack of local expertise, leading to reliance on costly external GPS data
which can be unreliable in these areas. A viable solution involves training
robots to develop their own maps and navigation skills over time by working
together with experienced companions, such as fellow robots that are familiar
with the location. This paper presents a novel method called VALUE, which
enables autonomous navigation in unknown urban areas without external GPS
data by creating a collaborative model that combines voting-based automatic
annotations from multiple robotic explorers. This approach ensures that robots
working together can efficiently plan and optimize their routes to annotate
environments in an exponential scale, rather than linearly, based on their
expertise levels and the complexity of the tasks. Our experiments using a
practical urban navigation scenario confirm the effectiveness of the proposed
method in supporting autonomous navigation for all participating robots. The
VALUE code has been made publicly available on GitHub.

In seismic deconvolution, inverse problem, and other areas, working with sparse signals is common to analyze signal characteristics. Theoretical optimization methods like Lasso, SPARSA, and others are widely applied for signal sparse enrichment. Notably, Lasso offers sparsity in both horizontal and vertical dimensions, however, limitations arise when dealing with non-uniformly spaced signals. To address this challenge, researchers have developed new methods, such as FOSTLasso and FOSTL1, which utilize a periodic model to account for the gaps in the grid, but these are impractical due to the complexity involved. The existing literature shows that non-uniform reconstruction can be performed using a tensor representation, however, the application is restricted to a specific pattern and does not generalize to other types. The approach is also non-applicable in cases of irregular 2D grids like the one seen in seismic reconstruction. This dissertation centers on the investigation of uniform integrability and its critical role in the theory of operator algebras. It begins by examining the historical development of this concept, starting with the original definition by Diestel and Uhl, and subsequent generalizations by Kumano-Gojo and Watanabe.  Building on their research, this dissertation introduces new theories of non- uniform integrability, and demonstrates their utility within the context of operator algebras.  Specifically, non-uniform integrability is proven to be a viable condition for the compactness of commutative operator algebras.  It is also recognized as an equivalent to semi-compactness in the scalar case, and this insight is extended to the operator algebra setting, leading to the identification of a localized version of semi-compactness.  Furthermore, this dissertation proves the equivalence between various types of non-uniform integrability, and also explores the link between this concept and the pseudo-Murray-von Neumann dimension in operator algebras, revealing that non-uniform integrability can be viewed as a generalized form of this dimension.  Finally, this dissertation introduces a set of criteria designed to establish the non-uniform integrability of sequences of operators, and these conditions are illustrated through a variety of examples.  One of the primary goals of this dissertation is to establish the relationship between non-uniform integrability and the almost periodicity and semi-compactness that have been previously identified as key descriptors of generalized Toeplitz algebras.  Specifically, this research demonstrates that non-uniform integrability is equivalent to semi-compactness, and also reveals that both of these conditions are equivalent to the generalized almost periodicity defined by Brattli and Larsen.  This research also identifies a localized version of semi-compactness and demonstrates its compatibility with the previously established equivalences.  In addition to these findings, this research introduces a set of criteria designed to establish the non-uniform integrability of sequences of operators, and by applying these conditions to the generalized Toeplitz algebras, this research is able to confirm prior findings while also revealing new insights.  Notably, this research confirms Brattli and Larsen's assertion that the generalized Toeplitz algebras are semi-compact, and also reveals that non-uniform integrability is equivalent to semi-compactness in the $C^*$-setting.  Furthermore, this research identifies a localized version of semi-compactness and confirms its compatibility with the previously established equivalences.

A comprehensive study on the behavior of multiple LEO spacecraft in various configurations has been conducted using a detailed model that takes into account the precise movements and interactions of individual spacecraft in the specific region. This model has been applied to a 67-satellite mini constellation in the LEO, spanning a wide latitude range, and the resulting data have been analyzed to understand space exploitation.

It's been observed that certain orbital positions hold a higher potential for successful deployment over a substantial period of time. Additionally, the research identifies critical areas and time periods where the risk of satellite collisions significantly increases, and the relative motion in the y-axis plays a crucial role in determining the likelihood of collision. 

This study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the challenges associated with space utilization and provide valuable insights for developers of small satellite systems, especially those aiming to establish constellations in the LEO. Furthermore, the research findings can be adapted and expanded to various other scenarios, including different orbital regions and configurations. 

Ultimately, the goal is to assist space technology developers in making well-informed design and operational decisions regarding their satellite constellations.

Experimental results using real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in reducing feature space uncertainty while increasing feature importance and system stability over traditional LIME-RS. Moreover, our findings highlight the state-of-the-art performance of the proposed algorithm in providing local explanations that meet these criteria. To achieve resilient machine learning under datashift, researchers have been exploring the use of information-theoretic approaches. A key concept, regional quotient, has been developed to measure the effectiveness of local training data in supporting generalization under distribution shift. Regional quotient helps to pin-point the most beneficial regions in sample-data distribution for use in sample-efficient learning. Furthermore, this method can guide the creation of tailored datasets for improving model performance. Despite the potential of regional quotient, its practical application remains unclear especially regarding which samples to draw from. This study investigates regional quotient's dependance on training sample data and sheds light on its statistical and computational requirements. Moreover, it demonstrates that utilizing regional quotient in model selection is beneficial in certain scenarios but does not always lead to improved generalization performance. Ultimately, this study provides guidelines on its practical application in machine learning settings. Our previous research demonstrated that calculating optimal transportation between two point clouds, using a precise or smoothed algorithm, takes linear time if the point clouds form a collinear triangle in dimension two. This finding built upon our prior discovery of the optimal transportation matrix being linearly dependent on triangle vertices for collinear triangles. In this study, the structure of the optimal transportation matrix was further explored, showing it can be expressed as a product of two matrices, each being a linear combination of the triangle's vertices. This product, or matrix decomposition, was achieved by applying G-Sylvester equations. Leveraging this product, we developed a new, linear-time algorithm to compute optimal transportation matrices. This algorithm first solves two linear systems to determine the coefficients of the optimal transportation matrix's product, and then solves two linear systems in a manner analogous to Sinkhorn's algorithm to obtain the matrix's per-coordinate values. We tested our algorithm using synthetic data and real images, finding it outperforms Sinkhorn's algorithm by achieving faster computation for collinear triangular distributions. Nonetheless, our algorithm falls short when distributions are non-collinear, becoming slower than Sinkhorn's algorithm in such scenarios. Furthermore, we validated the algorithm's effectiveness by verifying its predicted linear-time computational complexity and the accuracy of our algorithm using synthetic data and real images. Lastly, we utilized our algorithm to reveal new insights into the optimal transportation matrix's structure, finding it exhibits a tensor product factorization for multi-dimensional collinear triangular distributions. Overall, our findings indicate that the optimal transportation matrix's structure is highly dependent on the distribution's form, suggesting customized algorithms may be necessary to efficiently compute these matrices. Nonetheless, our algorithm offers unique benefits, encompassing both precise and statistical calculations, and can serve as a baseline for future work on algorithms for collinear triangular distributions. As expected, our algorithm fails to perform well on non-collinear triangular distributions, prompting future research into new methods for computing these matrices based on distribution structure. Moreover, our algorithm's success in other multi-dimensional scenarios remains untested, suggesting a need for further investigation into its performance in these cases. Finally, our algorithm's benefits extend beyond computational efficiency, allowing for new insights into the optimal transportation matrix's structure, and we hope to uncover even more characteristics that might be inherent in these matrices. If this assumption isn't satisfied, a significant issue occurs, resulting in inadequate local representation and consequently, poor prediction accuracy. To tackle this problem, we're proposing a novel statistical method called unevenNNA: uneven object nearest neighbor classification. UnevenNNA utilizes unevenness measures to detect disparities in data distribution and addresses the concern through two techniques: unevenness reduction and unevenness weighting. UnevenNNA combines these methods to enhance prediction accuracy when working with datasets that don't meet the requirement of even data distribution. Notably, unevenNNA maintains compatibility with existing statistical methods, including those developed by Horton and Kleinberg. Experimental outcomes revealed that unevenNNA outperforms comparable techniques, demonstrating its practical utility in real-world scenarios. A comprehensive implementation of unevenNNA is also available on GitHub. The research findings highlight the importance of object-level unevenness and provide a solution to improve near neighbor classification results. Specifically, unevenNNA improves accuracy by 20% in extreme cases. Furthermore, the research sheds light on the characteristics of unevenness, suggesting a distinct object-related phenomenon. Investigating this could lead to a deeper and more significant discovery. By analyzing the unevenness of real-world datasets, we can identify potential areas of improvement. A detailed description of unevenNNA is provided in this report, including key findings and recommendations for future research. The research aims to significantly contribute to the field by developing a statistical method to tackle the issue of accurate prediction with uneven data distribution. The dynamics of a liquid layer along a fiber are extensively utilized across various processes including, liquid jetting in fiber lasers and the formation of Taylor fibers during crystallization.  When this liquid layer experiences an external disturbance, it either remains stable or enters into a instability cycle characterized by the formation of periodic patterns along the fiber via a process known as the Rayleigh-Plateau (RP) instability.  Recent studies have highlighted the need for further understanding the mechanism by which a liquid layer along a fiber achieves dynamic stability through internal sliding while maintaining its overall integrity.  Consequently, it has been proposed that a slip-augmented version of the Rayleigh-Plateau instability is responsible for this mechanism.  Initially investigated theoretically, this phenomenon is now being further understood through experimental validation.  In this experiment, a polyethylene glycol-water-glycerol mixture is utilized in conjunction with hexane to study the onset of the slip-based instability through changes in viscosity while maintaining the interfacial tension at optimal levels.  Observations reveal the coexistence of two distinct forms of instability, a well-documented form characterized by the formation of convex droplets at lower viscosities and a previously unreported form characterized by the formation of neck-like structures at higher viscosities.  Notably, this latter form of instability exhibits dynamic stability through slip-induced instability when viscosity is increased beyond a certain threshold.  Consequently, this phenomenon is now being further understood through additional experimental and theoretical investigations into the mechanism by which slip affects the formation of stable convex droplets along a fiber through a slip-based instability mechanism. We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, demonstrating that any time-evolving function with Lipschitz norm less than one-half can be obtained as the temporal evolution of a initial function. Furthermore, we establish the optimal Lipschitz norm condition of one-half by proving that perturbing a Dirac mass by a distance of one-half yields the equation's solution. Subsequently, we extend these findings to include the more general Riemannian H-S equation on a flat, one-dimensional manifold by deriving the optimal Lipschitz norm, which is equal to one. Moreover, we demonstrate that any time-evolving function with a Lipschitz norm less than one can be obtained as the temporal evolution of a initial function. These results are significant, as they show that various known solutions of the H-S equation, including those derived from inversions and superpositions, satisfy the temporal Lipschitz condition. In fact, the study reveals that the H-S equation admits a vast, continuous family of solutions that include Dirac masses and their variously classified inversions and superpositions. In particular, the H-S equation is shown to admit solutions that include the Dym equation's soliton, the CH equation's soliton, and the $\sqrt{x}$ equation's soliton, among others. These solutions can be obtained as temporal evolutions of initial Dirac masses that are perturbed with specific distances. The distances for these specific solitons serve as evidence of the optimal Lipschitz norm conditions for the respective inversion and superposition problems. A reliable and consistent method of scoliosis evaluation using ultrasound imaging by inexperienced examiners is essential for effective detection. This study compares the accuracy of robotic ultrasound scanning, manually scanned images by physical therapists, and clinically assessed images by primary care providers in evaluating scoliosis using ScolioMan. The study analyzed curvature angles in 60 participants with scoliosis, finding that robotic scanning and manual scanning yielded similar results despite varying levels of examiner experience. Notably, robotic scanning exhibited minimal variation, accounting for only 5% of the total curvature angle measurements. In contrast, inexperienced examiners' manually scanned images correlated strongly with robotic scanning results, showing curves of 0.87 or higher. These findings support the use of robotic scanning for scoliosis evaluation, an effective and efficient tool that can also aid in training less experienced providers. Additionally, generating ScolioMan curves from manually scanned images is a reliable way to measure curvature angles, especially for those with less scanning experience. The consistency and accuracy demonstrated by robotic scanning and manual scanning with less experience suggest that these methods can be valuable tools in scoliosis evaluation. Further research is needed to assess the long-term effectiveness and usability of these techniques in clinical settings. However, the widely adopted Rapid Multipole Method approach, which efficiently calculates gravitational potentials, can sometimes result in artificial changes to angular momentum when non-axisymmetric terms are not accurately evaluated. Fluid-based systems often benefit from utilizing Koopman operator theory, which offers a powerful framework for analyzing them. The adaptive spectral Koopman (ASK) method has emerged as a promising approach for determining the action of the Koopman generator on observables within discrete data sets. However, certain applications necessitate exploring the Koopman generator in continuous domains. Although sparse-grid techniques can be employed in such cases, they introduce additional uncertainty, and their effects on AsK branching techniques and performance have yet to be investigated. In this study, we employ sparse-grid techniques to advance the AsK method by proposing two new approaches - sparse-grid adaptive spectral Koopman (SSAK) and sparse-grid adaptive spectral Koopman dynamic mode decomposition (SSAK-DMD). By leveraging the efficacy of AsK and the accuracy of sparse-grid techniques, our proposed frameworks have the potential to outperform existing methods in exploring the continuous action of the Koopman generator. Through numerical case studies and simulations, we evaluate the performance of SSAK and SSAK-DMD methods and assess their reliability and efficiency. Furthermore, we showcase the practical application of these methods in monitoring a real-world pump-turbine system. The findings of this research reveal that SSAK and SSAK-DMD methods significantly reduce the computational burden and data requirements, and can be effectively used to explore complex, high-dimensional systems. Moreover, they can provide accurate results without relying on complex observations, and their performance is comparable to that of the standard AsK method. Finally, these methods can successfully detect and analyze system nonlinearities, and their accuracy and stability are directly influenced by the selected observation points and time steps. Nonetheless, further research is necessary for integrating sparse-grid techniques into data-driven approaches for exploring the action of the Koopman generator in continuous domains. The detailed analysis and insights from this investigation may aid researchers and practitioners in exploring the potential of sparse-grid techniques to enhance data-driven methods for exploring the Koopman generator. The approach proposed in this study can significantly reduce the computational burden and data requirements for exploring the Koopman generator in continuous domains, and has the potential to be widely adopted in various engineering applications. It may also pave the way for integrating sparse-grid techniques into other data-driven methods for exploring the Koopman generator. A computational method, the Outward Complex Scaling Technique, is introduced to treat atomic and molecular systems under the influence of a strong direct current (DC) electric field. This approach overcomes the limitation of the Laplace operator by utilising an adaptive energy-dependent scaling transformation, effectively utilising a position-dependent scaling factor $s(\epsilon)$ that increases with increasing absolute energy $\epsilon$. The method employs a series solution for the wave function featuring terms with increasing powers of the scaling factor. A specially developed Outward Solution Generation Algorithm efficiently produces a well-conditioned non-Hermitian matrix for the coefficients of the wave function terms. The method avoids the problematic inward-going spectral issue typical of energy-dependent complex scaling transformations. By utilising an initial starting point with minimal kinetic energy, the Outward Complex Scaling Technique successfully yields the ground state wave function and energy for the hydrogen molecule ion in strong DC fields. Furthermore, this method accurately recreates the vacuum instability in the non-perturbative DC field potential of the hydrogen atom, thereby providing crucial insights for the study of high-order ionization in single and double electron systems. Ultimately, the method is poised to facilitate the exploration of novel quantum states arising from the interplay between electronic correlation and non-perturbative ionization in strong DC fields. The accompanying software code can be accessed via the repository located at https://github.com/stephencarrington/OutwardComplexScalingTechnique. A comprehensive open-source software suite for the numerical solution of Schrödinger equations in strong DC fields, incorporating the Outward Complex Scaling Technique and additional methods, can be found at https://github.com/stephencarrington/WallpaperStates. The software is compatible with high-performance computing environments. The method and accompanying software presented herein offer the capability to investigate a wide range of unexplored quantum states, encompassing systems of any size and configuration. Measurements of the $t\bar{t}$ production cross-section have been conducted using proton-proton collision data collected at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy with the ATLAS detector. In 2011, the total integrated luminosity of 25 $fb^{-1}$ was recorded. Differential cross-sections for $t\bar{t}$ events are investigated as functions of various kinematic factors. These include the rapidity and transverse momentum of the top quark, as well as several variables describing final states. Additionally, the probability of jets with more than four quarks is examined. Utilizing a leptonic decay method that takes into account both electron and muon decays of top quarks and accounting for detector inefficiencies using tag-and-probe techniques, the $t\bar{t}$ differential cross-sections are calculated. Based on these measurements, the $t\bar{t}$ production cross-section for proton-proton collisions is found to be $297 \pm 16 \pm 57 \pm 17$ $pb$, in line with the Standard Model prediction. Furthermore, using simulated data the expected precision in upcoming analyses is estimated. These data will be of great benefit to understanding the properties of the top quark and testing quantum chromodynamics, particularly at the two-loop level. For example, the measurement could be utilized to determine the pole mass of the top quark with a precision of 1.5 $GeV$. Other potential analyses are also explored to illustrate their impact on measuring the properties of the top quark. These data will significantly contribute to understanding the characteristics of the top quark. [Abstract]

Using an aggregation-dispersion model, we analyze a mix of aggregated data (e.g., train stations, schools) and GPS-derived, fine-grained mobility information (e.g., workplaces, recreation areas). Between March 2020 and February 2021, lower socioeconomic groups increasingly visited high-risk locations like grocery stores, while concurrently reducing their visits to low-risk spots, leading to a significant increase in risk exposure. Conversely, higher socioeconomic individuals maintained relatively stable interaction patterns during the pandemic, ultimately exacerbating income disparity in urban mobility and revealing a greater need for tailored, differentiated policy responses to address distinct socioeconomic effects. The algebraically special metrics, characterized by their unique geometric properties on the conformal sphere, are integrated with the Einstein C metric to create a consistent spacetime for ideal fluids with a negative cosmological constant. Effective digital urban planning is heavily reliant on high-quality spatial data, which facilitates decision-making, as cities are now managed as complex, interconnected systems. This research aims to address gaps in urban planning decision-support through spatial data customization and tailored analysis solutions. The investigation is centered on the potential integration of digital framework plans, with a focus on the spatial data types, architectures, and associated queries that are crucial for urban planning. A comparative analysis was conducted on spatial data types and approaches used in European cities, with the cities of Aarhus, Copenhagen, and Lund selected as the primary test cases. A proposed spatial data extension for the OSMOdom OSM database is presented, accompanied by an examination of query languages and practices that are commonly employed for analytical purposes. The solutions and strategies obtained can serve as a resource for other cities, allowing them to create custom spatial data and analysis approaches tailored to their unique needs. The research was presented to multiple cities, with the cities expressing interest in utilizing these solutions to enhance their urban planning processes. A conceptual framework for urban planning decision-support is also introduced, with the purpose of facilitating competitions, as well as enhancing the effectiveness of processing spatial data. This novel method considers the interactions between the probe, sample, and electromagnetic field using a hierarchical basis set decomposition method to efficiently account for high-frequency oscillations. The approach also utilizes density fitting to approximate the exact electronic properties of the probe and sample, while employing time-dependent density functional theory to simulate the sample's response to the probe's high-frequency oscillations. A series of applications, including simulations of bond stretching and cleavage, have demonstrated the method's effectiveness in accurately describing interactions, thereby paving the way for a comprehensive understanding of the chemical and electromagnetic influences in TERS. Ammonium sulfate (AS), a widely used compound in various applications, has exhibited anomalous behavior with a high temperature gradient in thermodynamic and dielectric properties. To clarify this phenomenon, we conducted an in-depth nuclear inelastic scattering measurement on a polycrystalline AS sample between 5 and 140 K in its high-temperature ferroelectric phase. Our analysis focused on the neutron excitation spectrum, density-of-states, and phonon mode distribution across the temperature range to provide a dynamic understanding of the system. We discovered that the high-temperature behavior can be attributed to a significant alteration in the low-energy vibrational mode density and entropy due to the engagement of AS's rotational degrees of freedom, particularly the mobility of ammonium ions. This explanation is supported by our density-of-states calculations using density functional theory and phonon mode analysis. We propose that the high-temperature gradient behavior can be attributed to a first-order structural phase transition at approximately 115 K, rather than a previously suggested presence of antiferroelectric and paraelectric domains. Overall, our results demonstrate that the high-temperature behavior can be accounted for by considering the general nature of AS's crystallographic and chemical properties, rather than requiring a unique analysis. By combining our findings with dielectric and calorimetric data from the literature, we present a comprehensive overview of AS's thermodynamic and dielectric properties, highlighting the system's complex behavior. Additionally, we compare these results to the behavior of isomorphous thermally stable compounds, such as potassium sulfate, providing valuable insights into the relationship between crystal chemistry and thermodynamic and dielectric properties. One potential implication of these insights could be to explore the use of AS as an artificial model system to study biologically relevant rotational degrees of freedom. By adjusting the chemical environment surrounding a molecule, it may be possible to influence the mobility of individual groups within a compound, which could provide valuable knowledge for the understanding and treatment of various biological and pharmaceutical processes. In summary, our research provides a detailed and accurate analysis of the thermodynamic and dielectric properties of AS, revealing the underlying source of its extensive entropy alteration. The study also sets out a general strategy for the analysis of thermodynamic and dielectric data, which could be applied to a broader range of crystal chemistries to explore the complex relationship between molecular structure and physical properties. The findings of this research could potentially contribute to a significant advancement in our understanding of crystal chemistry and molecular physics, while also offering valuable insights into biological and pharmaceutical relevant rotational degrees of freedom.

Furthermore, our results shed light on the importance of developing robust prediction error signals in the midbrain, which is critical for healthy and efficient learning processes. In various measurement procedures, limitations on resource usage result in measurement uncertainty, which must be addressed before a more accurate final measurement can be achieved. Current research has primarily focused on addressing uncertainty introduced during a single measurement step. We present a novel theoretical framework, the iterative Bayesian unraveling framework (IBUF), which enables the reduction of uncertainty stemming from any number of sequential measurement steps. We illustrate the IBUF by applying it to scenarios involving the detection of elusive entities, where we demonstrate its application on processes with limited resources, such as cat-squared to cat measurement, and identify the optimal conditions for achieving the highest possible final accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate, both mathematically and through simulation, that IBUF yields better results than a commonly employed two-step method based on maximum likelihood estimation. Our findings provide a potential solution for addressing practical measurement limitations. We also explore the theoretical boundaries of IBUF, along with potential avenues for further analysis. While theoretically ideal, using IBUF once or repeatedly may not be feasible due to practical constraints, which we also examine. We demonstrate, using simulations, the practical applicability of IBUF under real-world constraints before demonstrating its potential value in experiments involving quantum coherence. Overall, our work demonstrates that, even after initial measurement uncertainty, subsequent measurements can yield more accurate results than previously thought, which has significant implications across various fields. We have made the IBUF code and instructions publicly available.

In numerous research domains, datasets with named entity information are invaluable. The implementation of electronic health records has enabled healthcare providers to efficiently access patients' information. However, the initial data collection likely consisted of various unconnected systems, producing disparate datasets formatted for specific inquires. As a result, a typical patient's file comprises multiple formats such as free-text documents for clinical notes, structured data for lab results, imaging files, and anonymized personal identification numbers. A unified understanding of electronic health records can be achieved by integrating multiple datasets, leveraging the strengths of multiple algorithms, and fostering a collaborative ground for developing accurate predictive models. This research proposes a graph neural network called the Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network (DSGNN) (DSGNN model), capable of combining various EHR datasets of differing formats by constructing a diverse similarity graph. The model evaluates and combines the diversity of multiple similar graphs through the use of a sample transformation layer based on transformer. This ground-breaking ground-up diversity mechanism is essential for developing accurate graph neural network models. As a self-contained framework, the DSGNN model overcomes common challenges such as dataset integration, diversity, and accuracy by synthesizing a graph with combined EHR datasets. By doing so, the DSGNN model leverages diverse similarity for training and has demonstrated exceptional results across multiple supervised tasks. A baseline transformer model trained on a single dataset typically performs better than a baseline transformer model trained on the combined DSGNN graph. Nevertheless, when incorporating ground-up diversity, the DSGNN model performs significantly better than both the baseline models. Furthermore, the DSGNN model's diversity has a positive impact on domain experts, as it helps to identify novel relationships among entities. This study's success paves the way for a new dataset called the STUHealthcare Dataset, which contains a large collection of combined diverse graphs from 8 different healthcare datasets. Extracting building edges from satellite images is crucial for creating detailed building maps and databases. While deep learning methods have achieved significant advancements in edge detection, they are hampered by two primary limitations: the difficulty in replicating results across various datasets and platforms, and the lack of comprehensibility (interpretability). In an effort to address these issues, researchers have proposed a new edge detection method that leverages simplified models to analyze image textures. This approach utilizes two low-complexity filters to represent image textures as a combination of edges and surface patterns. By analyzing images through a variety of perspectives, corresponding to different filter orientations, the method can identify and refine edge structures. Experimental results, utilizing a widely available dataset for building edge detection, have demonstrated the proposed method's superiority over a leading deep learning model based on convolutional neural networks. In a notable comparison, the new method has successfully identified more than 95% of image edges with minimal class imbalance. Furthermore, the method's source code is publicly accessible and has been validated on multiple popular image processing platforms. In a subsequent investigation, researchers have successfully adapted the proposed method to incorporate temporal context, identifying and tracking Edges of Greater Semantic Value across multiple images. This work has significant implications beyond edge detection, with potential applications in a range of computer vision domains. The core of the proposed Edges of Greater Semantic Value algorithm consists of three low-complexity filters: constructing image texture patterns, analyzing orientation patterns, and combining these elements to create meaningful edges. By applying these filters in different orientations, the method can identify and refine Edges of Greater Semantic Value. In experiments, the Edges of Greater Semantic Value algorithm has demonstrated the ability to locate more than 96% of image edges with minimal class imbalance. Moreover, the method's interpretability has allowed for validation on multiple platforms, including a lightweight embedded device. The proposed Edges of Greater Semantic Value algorithm opens new avenues for research in this area and can be further adapted to suit specific application requirements. In the high-fluence X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) regime, the standard rate equation approach based on rate operators incorporating emission and absorption rates becomes ineffective due to the disappearance of a well-defined reference state, caused by an excessive number of emitted photons. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel framework for analyzing XAS data that systematically evaluates higher-order electron population states. By expanding the perturbation theory in the context of time-dependent perturbation theory, our formulation calculates higher-order transition rates in a well-defined quantitative framework. To simplify this analysis, we have also established a numerical integration method, which we have successfully applied to the analysis of the Au $L$-edge spectrum. By comparing our results with both experimental data and state-of-the-art time-resolved XAS measurements, we have found that our approach accurately captures the observed high-fluence phenomena. Specifically, we have observed that the transition from the ground state to the second excited state plays a crucial role in explaining the observed discrepancy at higher fluences. Moreover, our approach is not only applicable to the Au $L$ edge but can also be extended to the analysis of other $L_III$-$edge spectra, which exhibit even more complex behavior. The proposed method for analyzing higher-order transition rates, involving both three- and four-photon interactions, is expected to facilitate a deeper understanding of the nonlinear response of core electrons under intense X-ray radiation. The ability of these core electrons to withstand extremely high fluences paves the way for further exploration of the fundamental properties of electron liquids in this context. The advanced mathematical framework developed here significantly enhances our ability to analyze XAS data at high fluences, thereby significantly increasing the applicable fluence range from approximately millijoules per square centimeter to tens of kilojoules per square centimeter. The highest-order transition rate considered in this model is expected to set the standard for future analyses, opening up new possibilities for investigating the high-fluence behavior of electron populations in XAS experiments. The proposed mathematical model and associated methods are expected to be valuable resources for researchers working in the fields of XAS, ultrafast science, and core-level spectroscopy, facilitating a deeper understanding of the high-fluence behavior of electron populations. The direct relationship between high-fluence behavior and the fundamental properties of electron liquids makes this behavior a critical area of investigation for researchers seeking to gain insights into the fundamental origins of high-fluence phenomena. A critical capability in drone security is the ability to categorize different types of radio frequency (RF) modulation. Drifts and sudden changes in signal patterns caused by intruding utilizations can deceive conventional estimation techniques and lead them to inaccurately classify modulation types. To address this, we present an innovative method that utilizes multiple neural networks to classify modulation, even in the face of malicious attacks. By training and combining the strengths of individual networks via ensemble, we achieve a high level of resistance against sudden changes and malicious assaults. Through comprehensive testing, our proposed method demonstrates an 11% improvement in overall accuracy compared to current best practices. Additionally, it showcases a high level of resistance against sudden changes and malicious assaults. Furthermore, our results indicate that the proposed method can accurately categorize modulation in real-time, with an overall accuracy of 90% under real-world intruding utilizations. All experiments were conducted using an open-source testbed that mimics the real-world environment. This testbed allows us to simulate various RF signals and assess the performance of different classification methods. Our evaluation reveals that the proposed method's real-time accuracy outperforms current best practices by a significant margin. To promote reproducibility, all code and datasets used in this research are publicly available on our GitHub repository. By contributing these open-source tools to the security community, we hope to stimulate further research and collaboration to develop robust modulation categorization methods. These tools can be applied not only to RF signals, but also to other domains such as spectroscopy and time series analysis. Moreover, we believe that the success of our proposed method can be a benchmark for the security community to strive for in developing generalizable solutions to classification problems. Previous studies on multiple sclerosis (MS) lesion segmentation have concentrated on one-way transfer, where data from MS clinics is used to improve training or testing performance. To address the scarcity of MS data through streaming new data, we investigate the potential of two-way transfer in the MS lesion segmentation task. MS lesions exhibit diverse appearances in different clinics, which poses a challenge for one-way transfer. This study compares three approaches to addressing this issue: using a pre-trained model, continuous learning, and training from scratch. MS lesions in different clinics exhibit distinct characteristics, making continuous learning a viable option. Our study evaluates these approaches using a publicly available MS lesion segmentation dataset from four clinics. The results indicate that a continuous learning strategy incorporating data decomposition is well-suited to addressing the issue of varying MS lesion appearances across clinics. When continuous learning is applied, the performance boost can be as high as 8.4% in terms of dice similarity coefficient (DSC). The findings also reveal that the combination of models from multiple clinics achieves better performance than a pre-trained model or a model trained from scratch, even when the performance gain is small. Moreover, the research highlights the importance of the design of continuous learning in the absence of a well-defined theoretical framework. I'll discuss how to identify identical entities within two datasets that have been pre-labeled, a problem that can be applied to various scenarios. In many cases, these entities aren't randomly distributed and often belong to distinct categories. By considering dual comparisons, we can reduce the extensive calculation required for paired items in original datasets. Dual comparisons involve comparing two sets of pre-labeled items from separate pre-labeled collections. While this method was initially proposed as a means to reduce the dimensionality of data for classification, it can also be used to identify the within-category identical entities in dual datasets. By combining dual comparisons with model training, we have developed an approach to automatically identify the within-category identical entities in dual datasets without extensive manual labor. This new method is efficient, computationally speaking. In addition to identifying identical entities, our approach can also determine the number of items in each dataset and calculate their similarity. This can be further applied to a variety of scenarios such as automatically combining the reviews of a single product listed on different online marketplaces, identifying the within-category identical entities in dual datasets for model training, and verifying the accuracy of online product information by cross-checking it with other online marketplaces, all of which were previously done manually due to the within-category identical entities in the datasets. By leveraging dual comparison, we can automate these tasks. Our proposed method is based on the idea that dual comparison can be used to identify the within-category identical entities in dual datasets without the need for extensive manual labor. This can be achieved by training the dual datasets using dual comparison and automatically identifying the within-category identical entities in the datasets. By doing so, our approach can efficiently calculate the similarity of the identified entities in the dual datasets and automatically combine the reviews of a single product listed on different online marketplaces. This can be further applied to verify the accuracy of online product information by cross-checking it with other online marketplaces, all of which were previously done manually. By leveraging dual comparison, we can automate these tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. The existence of Infrared Dark Nebulae (IDNs) proves that the dense cores responsible for forming massive stars still remain undetected. To understand the evolution of massive star forming cores, it's crucial to study the properties of these dense cores. We conducted a study of the IDN within the Dragon molecular cloud using science-ready ALMA images from the ALMA Science Pipeline. We employed an unsupervised machine learning approach to identify dense core properties and applied the RED analysis tool to determine spectral line energy distribution characteristics. The analysis revealed five cores within the Dragon IDN, indicating it is actually a complex of dense cores, rather than a single object. We successfully applied the RED analysis tool to IDNs and measured the physical conditions and masses of the cores, revealing mass distributions that suggest mass loss in the cores over time. By comparing our findings to simulated data, we determined the stage of core development in the IDNs and the Dragon, indicating the IDN complex is in the advanced phase of core development. Our study implies massive star forming cores undergo dynamic changes, similar to isolated star forming cores, advancing from protostellar condensation to massive core collapse stage. However, unlike isolated cores, IDNs in molecular clouds undergo mass loss due to external pressure. We propose that the IDN in the Dragon, which has not yet formed a massive star, may contain the next massive star forming core. Its potential for massive star formation makes the non-protostellar IDN unique and worthy of further observation. To advance our understanding of massive star forming cores, we suggest monitoring the IDN in the Dragon to monitor its evolution into a massive star forming core. Future follow-up observations should confirm whether the IDN forms a massive star by observing the emergence of massive star signatures. Future follow-up observations of IDNs across the galaxy could reveal whether all IDNs are in the early stages of massive star formation. Additionally, we suggest that the IDN formation could be influenced by the dynamics in the Dragon, which may be part of a larger larger phenomenon, such as a shock from a nearby young stellar object that triggered the formation of the dense cores through cooperative and competitive processes. Further studies of the dynamics in the Dragon can confirm whether the IDN formation is part of widespread star forming activity in the region.

The theoretical framework of Primordial Black Hole dark energy is gaining traction due to its potential for resolving long-standing cosmological issues. However, the associated equations are complex and require numerical resolution. A computational model, PopSyCLE, has been developed to simulate early cosmological events such as black hole formation, which we detail in this paper along with an explanation of how the model is incorporated into a larger cosmological framework to study the evolution of primordial black holes. Our PopSyCLE model utilizes a simplified approach to incorporate statistical variations in initial conditions, which we apply to a cosmological dataset to demonstrate its capabilities. The outcome of these simulations reveals a deeper understanding of the evolution of primordial black holes and their potential to satisfy various cosmological requirements. Specifically, our models indicate that a primordial black hole-based dark energy scenario can be consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background and measurements of the universe's current expansion rate. The simulations presented here mark a significant step forward in preparing theoretical models to account for precise measurements from future experiments, whether they be observations or analyses of gravitational signals. A major advantage of our approach is that a primordial black hole-based dark energy model that meets observational requirements can generate a self-consistent cosmological scenario by fitting data on the growth of structures across various scales. Specifically, our models are consistent with measurements of the density of dark energy and the gravitational potential in our universe. The evolution equations for a primordial black hole-based dark energy scenario are found to be similar to those of a cold dark matter model, but with distinct equations describing the evolution of pressure and energy in a primordial black hole. By propagating uncertainties in initial conditions and simulating the evolution of a primordial black hole-based dark energy universe, our PopSyCLE model reveals a range of possible cosmological scenarios and confirms that a correct model can be identified from a large set of possible models through a best-fit analysis. The model's potential for identifying statistical variations in initial conditions that affect the formation and growth of primordial black holes is a significant outcome. Specifically, our model's ability to generate a correct cosmological scenario with a correct value of the Hubble constant has been demonstrated. The model's potential for identifying the correct value of parameters related to the formation of primordial black holes by fitting gravitational signals from the main gravitational source of these black holes and its potential for identifying the correct value of parameters related to the evolution of a dark matter universe are significant outcomes. The model's potential for simulating a dark matter universe with various types of dark energy has been demonstrated

We focus on the efficiency of language model fine-tuning parameters, an important consideration especially when working with large pre-trained models. Our investigation indicates that fine-tuning not only changes the final output layer but also modifies the hidden representations within the model. Consequently, adjusting model parameters alone may not be enough to elicit meaningful responses from the model. A potential remedy for this issue is the use of "unique token adaptation", which involves introducing new unique tokens to the model and fine-tuning the embeddings associated with these tokens. By doing so, the model can effectively fine-tune its hidden representations while minimizing parameter adjustments. We have demonstrated the efficacy of unique token adaptation in various tasks, including sentiment analysis, word sense disambiguation, and machine translation, and have found that a smaller number of unique tokens can be just as effective as a larger number while reducing the memory requirements of the model. Additionally, unique token adaptation has been found to be beneficial in the context of data augmentation, as it allows the model to recognize new concepts introduced during the augmentation process. Our results suggest that unique token adaptation is a useful technique for fine-tuning language models in a resource-efficient manner. A publicly available implementation of our method can be found at https://github.com/jpgard/unique_token_adaptation. Experimental evaluations across six language pairs confirm the substantial improvements yielded by LFA, which showcases its potential as a widely applicable and efficient NMT advancement. Additionally, our proposed method is compatible with a variety of production techniques and can serve as a significant contribution to the NMT research community. Text-video retrieval has gained significant interest in recent years, with the main goal of locating corresponding video clips for a given text input. This task is complex due to the large gap between text and visual inputs, as well as the requirement for precise alignments between them. To tackle this issue, we developed TS2-Net, a novel model that incorporates token shift and choice operations into a single transformer framework. This model consists of three key components: 
  1) A pre-processing module to split the text and visual features into smaller chunks, 
  2) A processing module that performs token shift and choice operations to capture text and visual cues, and 
  3) A post-processing module that re-ranks the initial top results to obtain the final outputs. Additionally, we developed two novel operators within the token shift and choice framework: 
  4) Intra-cross-attention to mine intra-token cues, 
  5) Temporal fusion to combine spatial-temporal features, and 
  6) Text-vision multi-modal feature fusion to integrate the text and visual features. We tested TS2-Net's performance on various video datasets, including activity recognition, movie identification, and MSRVTT, with the results indicating its state-of-the-art performance on MSRVTT and MSVD. This model is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/zhangwenjun2018/TS2-Net. Furthermore, our model secured 2nd place in the activity detection track of the I3D-ACE challenge at MM 2021. EKG signals hold valuable information about a person's well-being, and analyzing them can provide vital insights into cardiovascular health. Specifically, interpreting EKG signals can help identify abnormal heart rhythms known as arrhythmias. In this research paper, we explore how to quantify the time intervals between EKG signal peaks to diagnose arrhythmias. Previous studies have relied on traditional machine learning methods, but these approaches are often overly complex and imprecise. By contrast, we introduce a novel, simplified model called Tiramisu, which achieves accuracy without the need for extensive data preprocessing or elaborate neural networks. Our research demonstrates that the Tiramisu model exhibits exceptional performance, achieving 97.7% accuracy in predicting EKG signal intervals of normal heart rhythms and 93.5% accuracy in predicting abnormal rhythms. Additionally, the model's simplicity allows for faster processing times, making it well-suited for practical applications. Notably, the Tiramisu model's performance outshines existing literature in this domain. Furthermore, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance while using significantly fewer parameters, which has important implications for real-world implementations. Lastly, our model's performance characteristics reveal that the Tiramisu model's predictions for shorter EKG sample sequences (up to 8 samples) exhibit relatively lower accuracy due to the challenges associated with predicting initial signal patterns. Nonetheless, the Tiramisu model's predictions for longer sequences demonstrate a marked improvement in accuracy. These findings suggest that the Tiramisu model's accuracy can be further enhanced by incorporating additional sequential data points. In conclusion, our model's performance outshines existing literature in this domain, which can lead to new, simplified arrhythmia detection methods using EKG signals. These models have the potential to save lives by helping healthcare professionals diagnose abnormal heart rhythms more effectively. Moreover, our model's performance can be expanded to other sequential data sets such as e.g. processing EKG signals of longer duration, which will be explored in the future studies. We have developed a stochastic algorithm, passing-based Tensor SVD, to calculate a component of the singular value decomposition of a low-rank tensor. By randomly permuting the indices of the tensor and calculating approximations to the singular values and vectors in iterations, similar to the stochastic SVD, we can obtain an accurate estimate of a singular value and its corresponding u and v components after a certain number of iterations. We have shown that the number of iterations needed to achieve a certain level of accuracy depends on the rank of the tensor and the desired level of accuracy, and not on its size. We have also proven that the expected level of accuracy is related to the number of iterations. We have provided theoretical bounds on the number of iterations needed to achieve a certain level of accuracy, as well as methods for combining the results of multiple passes. We have tested the algorithm on synthetic and real-world datasets in various domains, including physics, chemistry, and biology. We have compared it to a non-parallel method and demonstrated that it is possible to achieve the same level of accuracy using significantly fewer iterations when working with large datasets, thus allowing for parallel processing. We have also proposed a speedup strategy based on an optional count of passes. We have shown that the algorithm is scalable and can handle large datasets by gradually increasing the number of processors from 1 to 32 in parallel computations, ultimately achieving a speedup of almost 25 times compared to non-parallel method on a dataset with 4,096 elements. Finally, we have applied the algorithm to calculate a component of the singular value decomposition of a chemical dataset of large size (134,217,728 elements) using 32 processors. Using 40,000 passes, we have calculated an accurate estimate of all singular values and their corresponding u and v components, demonstrated to be correct by verifying the rank of the tensor using multiple methods. We have further validated the results by performing multiple internal cross-validation procedures and applying the algorithm to various real-world datasets in the field of materials science, neuroscience, and genomics to obtain accurate estimates of the singular values and their corresponding u and v components. Overall, the passing-based Tensor SVD algorithm is a robust and reliable method that can be used to calculate a component of the singular value decomposition of a tensor with low-rank structure, even in the presence of missing data. It is a versatile and efficient tool, applicable to different types of data such as tensors with rectangular or square profiles. It can be used in various fields, including physics, chemistry, biology, materials

A recent study on the $^7$H nucleus treated as an excess neutron in the $^3$H nucleus has led to a revised consideration of the ground state. Considering that $^7$H has a large neutron separation energy, the idea that its ground state could be similar to a $^3$H nucleus structure with four neutrons added becomes plausible. This suggestion is based on the concept that if neutrons are added to a nucleus near its drip line, the resulting neutrons integrate into the wave function of the existing nucleus and form a one-neutron-hole system. This concept has guided a search for indications in $^3$H+$n_n$ systems that they exist in a $^7$H ground state. To investigate this possibility, the paper reviews and analyzes data from two experiments: $^3$H($d$, $p$)$^4$H at 20 MeV incident energy and $^4$H at 13.3 MeV incident energy, where the second involved an off-axis measurement that allowed for $^7$H ground state resonance analysis. The paper presents original data and provides new resonance analysis in the $^3$H-$d$ reaction that was not previously examined. As a result, the data suggest the possible existence of $^7$H ground states at two different masses, $m_7=5.99\pm0.01$ (amu) and $m_7=6.03\pm0.01$ (amu), each with a width of about 120 (keV) that meets the condition for a $^7$H ground state resonance. A width of about 120 (keV) for the $^7$H ground state is also consistent with that of $^3$H at 16.3 (MeV) in the $d$-$p$ scattering process. The data from this measurement are consistent with those from the off-axis measurement for analytical calculations of the $^7$H ground state. This study demonstrates the resolution of the Nirenberg problem for minimal hypersurfaces in the half-sphere - a case previously unexplored. Notably, our solution yields minimal, non-trivial disconnections of the half-sphere, as well as new, non-trivial minimal hypersurfaces that intersect the sphere's equator. Our approach employs the catenary surfaces as a key component to resolve the Nirenberg problem. These catenary surfaces are obtained by specifying mean curvature function $H$ on the half-sphere $S^n_+, r$, based on its distance from the equator, resulting in a mean curvature-0 subsurface. Such structures are akin to a "half-clifford torus" when $n=2$, and they naturally feature a boundary $S^{n-1}_+$ as a 1-dimensional sphere. Importantly, our solution for $H$ on the half-sphere $S^n_+, r$ does not rely on symmetry, given that the boundary mean curvature $\sigma_{S^nx}$ at any point $x$ on $S^n_+, r$ is simply the 0 component of the total surface mean curvature $\sigma_{S^n}x$ on the complete sphere $S^n$. In turn, this allows us to derive a condition for identifying a minimal hypersurface $M^m$ within $S^n_+, r$, as follows: for any point $x$ on the equator $S^1$, the total surface mean curvature $\sigma_{S^n}x$ must possess 0 as its final $n-1$ components. Consequently, the obtained condition gives rise to a non-trivial, connected minimal hypersurface $M^m$ in $S^n_+, r$ for any point $x$ on the equator $S^1$ with the total surface mean curvature $\sigma_{S^n}x$ having a non-zero $n-1$ component. A critical challenge in machine learning is effectively learning representations. A well-suited framework for this task involves a system of dynamic equations known as flows, which can be seen as a sequence of linear transformations where each step considers previous ones. When used in representation learning, these equations facilitate the exchange of information between successive steps. However, the problem becomes complex and difficult to solve when the number of steps increases due to the interdependence of the steps. A solution to this challenge has been proposed in the paper by introducing a variational approach that reformulates the problem using the Sinkhorn distance, thereby simplifying the original optimization problem into a more manageable least-squares problem with a simpler structural context. This reformulation accelerates the optimization process and allows for the incorporation of additional constraints on the step-wise transformations. A comprehensive set of experimental evaluations demonstrates the performance superiority of the proposed method compared to several established techniques. Additionally, the research provides clear guidelines and recommendations for selecting the optimal parameters for the proposed method. A suitable interpretation of the proposed approach has been provided in the domain of information theory, specifically in light of the theoretical results by Tameling et al. and the more recent research by James et al. regarding the generalizability of deep neural networks. Specifically, the research provides clear answers to the following key questions: What types of datasets have the optimal representation, and why? What dataset size and structure are required to achieve an optimal representation, and why? A related open question has also been posed in the conclusion section. This research examines the Betti numbers of Gaussian trajectories in the sparse condition. Under the assumption that the exponential growth of the kernel has a mean less than one, we prove that the expected Betti numbers for large sample sizes n display a linear relationship with the logarithm of n. We further derive the leading coefficients for these linear relationships. Additionally, under the same assumptions, we analyze the limiting Betti numbers and determine the vector field's functional determinant in the limit. We back our findings with simulation results. This research builds on previous works by Edwards and Kozlov (1994), Edwards (1997), and Bera (2018) in the dense case, using a different approach which involves determining the asymptotic counting function for the number of holes as a function of n. This approach involves applying the Stein's Equation to a generating function, previously utilized by Bera (2018) in a different context, to derive a key equation relevant to homological percolation. By solving this equation, we derive a fundamental relation between the kernel's functional renewal process and the critical exponent for homological percolation. We leverage this relation to derive a formula for the fundamental measures and exercise the application of these results through homological percolation calculations on Gaussian kernels. Lastly, we extend these results to cover the scenario of multi-dimensional Gaussian trajectories. Please note that due to the scope of our research notes' limitations, the homological homogenization method used in this work is only briefly outlined. A more in-depth explanation can be found in separate research papers. The methods and findings from this study have been previously discussed in a lecture series by the author. Current methods involve time-consuming 3D simulations or expensive, high-precision sensors. We introduce SEIA, a groundbreaking system that utilizes a single image to calculate the necessary camera adjustments, using features detected within that image combined with a trained model. We focus on learning the inverse dynamics model of a physical system by incorporating constrained reinforcement learning. Building upon the system's pre-trained forward model, we utilize interaction data to adjust the learned parameters. Our reinforcement learner explores the space of model adjustments, but its actions are restricted by the pre-existing forward model. This constrained optimization yields a more efficient exploration, requiring fewer samples to achieve similar performance as traditional off-policy reinforcement learning. Furthermore, our method simplifies off-policy reinforcement learning by integrating the pre-existing forward model, eliminating the need for environment resets. The combined approach accelerates the learning process by minimizing sample complexity. The proposed method is validated by successful inverse dynamics learning for multiple physical systems in experimental settings. Our findings demonstrate that utilizing existing knowledge can streamline the learning process and achieve more efficient exploration. The introduced framework is versatile and can be applied to a broad range of problems, including robot motion learning and control. Moreover, our results provide sample complexity analysis for off-policy reinforcement learning when combined with pre-existing forward models. Furthermore, DR2 has enabled researchers to explore the astrophysical implications of their findings, particularly regarding the population of extremely faint stars, a byproduct of this mission.
