Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are highly valued for their ability to solve complex equations within physics and engineering, combining data from both internal neural networks and external experimental data. As these networks increasingly rely on deep learning for increased flexibility, there is a significant concern regarding their lack of interpretability. This problem persists even when weakly regularized PINNs, which are more susceptible to overfitting in small datasets. To solve this issue, we propose an innovative method for accurately estimating PINN's posterior error. This method involves generating approximate solutions by PINNs with minimal added regularization, and subsequently applying a tailored analysis to quantify the resulting approximation error. Experiments using both synthetic and real-world data confirm that these suggested adjustments can effectively mitigate overfitting in PINNs, and reveal that their performance can be significantly enhanced by properly addressing model uncertainty. This enhancement is achieved without implementing additional regularization methods. Furthermore, the results illustrate that by incorporating data normalization, which is a fundamental aspect of most machine learning techniques, PINNs can accurately predict quantities with arbitrary units. Overall, the proposed approach facilitates a deeper and more comprehensive understanding of PINNs' underlying behavior. This insight is made possible by measuring the discrepancy between predicted and actual outputs at prediction time, and by analyzing the corresponding approximating solutions. This method is versatile, and can be applied to a wide range of PINNs, including those involving partial differential equations with various types of boundary conditions. Last but not least, the proposed approach is available at https://github.com/ghassan-shep/ambiguous-pinn. This resource allows for reproducing the results, and aids in further investigating the subject. For instance, it reveals that when dealing with multi-fidelity data, the lower-fidelity approximations should be viewed as solutions to distinct PDEs, rather than as an approximation error. This insight is consistent with the proposed analysis. Moreover, the proposed method is not only beneficial for gaining insight into the behavior of the learning process, but also improves the quality of the learned solutions, and their practical applicability. Notably, these results confirm that properly addressing model uncertainty can effectively mitigate overfitting in small datasets. One of the key implications of these findings is that when working with small datasets, one should not solely rely on the predicted outputs. Rather, it is advisable to consider the resulting approximation error, and to understand that this error is estimated based on the suggested methods in this research. These methods are not unique to PINNs, and can be applied to a wide range of other machine learning techniques

Deep neural networks are exceptionally versatile, but they have a significant flaw: they consistently perform poorly when given data that has been compromised. The process of contamination involves introducing malicious patterns or noise into a dataset, which is given to the model to hinder its ability to make accurate predictions. This particular study delves into the manipulation of datasets through contamination, graph classification, and reinforcement learning models built on Graph Neural Networks. The research uses contamination methods involving linear regression, rotational attacks, and random node contamination in datasets for GNNs, as well as exploring the potential to adapt these methods to the field of reinforcement learning, where self-play is a norm. The goal of this work is to examine the effects of contamination on model performance, the efficacy of remedies such as mixing with unpolluted data, and the development of a simple rotational contamination method applicable to RL models. The research will focus on the binary classification of graphs, employing the Open Graph Benchmark for evaluation. The findings indicate that graph classification performance is severely compromised even with a small percentage of contaminated data. However, the exploration also reveals possibilities for GNNs to achieve robust performance against rotational contamination attacks. The research also introduces a novel and highly effective robust training approach applicable to the field of reinforcement learning. The robustness of RL models can be improved by unpolluted data mixing, and the research also opens up avenues for addressing similar challenges in the domain. The research will be made accessible through a repository at https://github.com/andre-mendes/Graph-GNNs-Robustness. The research will be shared at IJCAI 2021. We introduce an novel technique to bridge the gap between speech and text representations through a cycle-consistency inter-domain penalty. Although previous approaches using cycle losses yield comparable results with professional datasets, training in this manner is impractical due to the extensive required for optimal performance. To address this challenge, we leverage a moderately sized auxiliary dataset with synchronized audio and transcript pairs to fine-tune a pre-trained end-to-end automatic speech recognition model. We evaluate our approach on the MIT dataset and a 300-hour extension of Librispeech, achieving a significant reduction in auxiliary dataset size needed to match the performance of professional datasets from 2000 to only 150 hours. To further augment our results, we employ an instance penalty technique to enhance model generalizability, ultimately yielding an improved CER of 12.64% on the MIT test set, outperforming the baseline CER of 13.25%. We also report a CER reduction of 4.75% and 1.75% on the Librispeech dev-clean and dev-other sets, respectively, compared to the Librispeech baseline CER. To the best of our knowledge, this work pioneers the application of the instance penalty to end-to-end automatic speech recognition for speech enhancement tasks. We publicly release our code and the pre-trained model for the community to reproduce our results. In addition, we contribute a new dataset, "diabi", consisting of 183 hours of speech with associated transcripts, to support the advancement of end-to-end automatic speech recognition models. Our approach tackles the challenge of detecting people in diverse settings, even when the original model is not familiar with the new environment. The size of the detection box is a valuable piece of information that contains valuable data, but it is often disregarded in existing techniques. In our work, we assign significance to box shape analysis as a distinguishing feature that can accommodate varying densities of people across different settings. A novel metric, known as Box Re-Ranking (BRR), is presented to eliminate incorrect positive associations. By discarding box shapes that are uncommon in people clusters and retaining those that are typical, BRR effectively reduces false positives. In addition, we design a feature representation with a simplified structure, called Correlation Suppression by Orthogonal Distribution (CSOD), to capture essential spatial relationships between people and eliminate unnecessary variables. A distinctive characteristic of CSOD is the separation of features into two subgroups: one focused on distinct individuals and the other focused on overall patterns. A weight adjustment mechanism is then applied to mitigate interference from the distinct subgroup while highlighting relevant information from the overall patterns subgroup. The combination of CSOD and BRR results in a powerful, unsupervised method for improving people detection in diverse settings. Comprehensive testing using seven diverse datasets shows that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. Initially, an investigation into the differences between neural networks used for audio and image analysis was conducted. Next, a simple method to convert audio representations into an image-like format was developed. Furthermore, research into multi-scale autoencoders was performed to create an audio representation suitable for enhancement. Building on this, a complex multi-scale autoencoder was developed, and its decomposition into separate frequency bands was done using the Mellin transform. Finally, an analysis-bypass vocoder was implemented to generate audio representations from compressed features. The findings suggest that image-like representations can be effective for audio enhancement and that novel feature extraction methods are valuable additions to this field. Moreover, an ideal representation for audio enhancement via neural networks has yet to be discovered. Consequently, the development of more complex multi-scale autoencoders and novel analysis methods could lead to significant advancements in this area. Our primary objective is to understand the impact of inaccurate simulation of ball release points on throwing gestures in virtual characters. To achieve this, we have developed FauxThrow, a method for producing false throwing movements where the character's arm follows a typical throwing pattern but the ball does not follow through correctly after release. This artificial behavior in characters' movements enables more precise evaluation methods for automated evaluation of virtual character animations. Specifically, our approach involves generating faux throws using a combination of two techniques: altering the pose of the character's arm to match a typical throwing pose and adjusting the position of the ball using a constraint that simulates a correct throw, but applies an artificial force preventing it from following through. By studying FauxThrow, we have investigated various aspects of this behavior, including the effect of different timing of when the ball's constraint is applied, the visual characteristics of the resulting faux throws, and how different types of releases (e.g. overarm vs underarm) affect the behavior. Our research has demonstrated that with sufficient practice, humans can become proficient at detecting these artificial movements during casual observations, but not when the practice involves intentionally searching for the faux throw. Furthermore, our approach allows for the development of more accurate methods for evaluating virtual character animations using a combination of practice-based evaluation and machine learning. FauxThrow has also highlighted several common characteristics of these artificial movements, including the ball appearing to stop mid-air, changing trajectory, and failing to reach the target location. To address these issues, we have proposed multiple methods for correcting the ball's position and motion, including re-throwing, re-impact, re-trajectory, and a combination of these techniques. Ultimately, our approach has allowed for the significant improvement of the accuracy of virtual character animation evaluation, specifically in terms of identifying when a throw occurs and the accuracy of the ball's final position. Our research has further demonstrated that by combining our approach with a pre-existing evaluation method, the accuracy of the evaluation can be improved from 28% to 57%, bringing it closer to the accuracy of human evaluation, which is approximately 70%. This improvement in accuracy is particularly notable as human accuracy varies between 50% and 85% depending on the specific evaluation method used. Consequently, our research has identified specific areas of study required to bridge the remaining gap in the accuracy of the evaluation, which is in the process of being investigated. To combine the abilities of neural machine translation and syntactic parsing, a new decoding method is proposed that builds upon an existing tree structured neural machine translation model by incorporating syntactic links. This linked model redefines the decoding process, splitting it into two parts: first, determining a translation sentence based on the input and syntactically correct state, and second, adjusting the state to ensure syntactic correctness while preserving the translation. When the model falls back on the default case, the state cannot be adjusted further, resulting in a sentence that is grammatically incorrect but syntactically correct. This model's effectiveness was tested using Chinese-English data sets from the NIST 2002-2003 Neural Machine Translation competitions, yielding a significant improvement in translation accuracy and a lesser, though still noticeable, decrease in overall accuracy due to the incorporation of syntactic guidance. Additionally, the model performed well in identifying grammatically correct syntactic links and a baseline study on the CoNLL 2017 data set demonstrated its capacity to improve parsing accuracy when translation is prioritized above grammatical correctness. A thorough analysis of the model's behavior was also provided. The source code for this model can be found at https://github.com/jjadergolam/LinkNMt. Furthermore, due to the model's intricate nature, a simplified variant is proposed for less experienced users, yielding comparable results to the full model in both translation and syntactic guidance. This simplified variant merges the translation and syntactic correctness adjustments into one decoding step, eliminating the model's complexity while still yielding improved overall accuracy. The model's simplified variant exhibits a mean average precision of 43.7% in translation and 73.4% in syntactic guidance, marking it suitable for practical applications in both translation and parsing. In astrophysical environments, small molecular molecules interact with larger molecular ions, leading to the release of binding energies when they dissociate. To better understand and accurately model this process, a comprehensive quantum chemical study of binding energy distributions is necessary. To facilitate further research in the astrochemical community, we present a new database containing binding energy distributions for various large molecular cations. We employed high-level quantum mechanical methods to determine the binding energies of 12 different hydrogen-containing molecular cations, calculating thousands of individual binding energies and their associated probability distributions. We then trained an artificial neural network, using a larger dataset from a theoretical study and including additional molecules not previously considered, to predict its own probability distributions. We subsequently determined the probability distributions for 25 more molecules not initially included in the original study. We make both the database and our code available for download, allowing for potential future expansions with experimental and other theoretical data. We use an example case to highlight the importance of accurately modeling probability distributions, showing that both average binding energies and the corresponding standard deviations obtained from the database and artificial neural network predict that deuterium is more tightly bound to the molecule than hydrogen. Nevertheless, employing standard deviations alone is insufficient to capture the extent of molecular coverage, and we observe that some molecules have a significant amount of mass that is lost during dissociation, in addition to the primary fragments. We suggest that future research should account for this significant mass loss when reporting results. We also compare our findings with a simplified model, such as that based on the continuous model, and recommend that results are reported with a range of binding energies rather than a single value. Moreover, when comparing with experimental data, it should be recognized that a lack of agreement does not necessarily mean that the calculated binding energies are incorrect. The presence of ambiguous words (also known as heteroglossial ambiguity) in a text can alter its categorization, leading to a less accurate classification once it is removed. To address this issue, our research presents a new method for enhancing the stability of a classifier against the potential for ambiguous words that might be specific to certain categories. This approach involves creating multiple classifiers, each of which is trained on a modified version of the original dataset, to one of several predetermined term counts. When classifying a new text, the classification results from all these modified datasets are combined to produce the final classification outcome. To implement this method, our technique can automatically identify and flag ambiguous words within a text based on their frequency and occurrence in multiple categories. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in mitigating the negative impact of ambiguous words, and demonstrate that our method outperforms a competing approach (LSI) in most cases. Furthermore, our approach can be considered a form of semantic representation for text categorization, and we found that a method which rewrites text to reduce heteroglossial ambiguity does not have the same level of performance as our approach which targets specific categories. Overall, our method can be considered an efficient form of noise-immunity training data modification for text categorization. The technique was tested using datasets in Japanese and Arabic languages, and most of the research was focused on Japanese datasets. An implementation of the technique can be found at http://www.johnmyers.org/sibylvar/. In the realm of machine learning, the concept of meta-learning involves training general-purpose algorithms that enable these algorithms to learn from experience. This research targets fundamental questions within meta-learning, particularly regarding whether meta algorithms can develop a basic understanding of the underlying structure of their learning process. To address this, we investigate whether meta algorithms can recognize linear relationships between sequential updates of model parameters during learning, which are considered fundamental representations of adaptation. This study presents a range of challenges, starting with the simplest case of learning linear illustrations, and then progressing to more complex scenarios involving multiple linear components, hidden adaptations, and obscured parameter evolutions. To resolve these challenges, we propose new problems, as well as a suite of benchmark datasets, and the DiffDif model. The last model variant, which stands for Differences Make a Difference, is specifically designed to capture the fundamental characteristics of parameter changes during learning. The model's design is informed by analytical findings on the nature of these changes, which are then experimentally validated. The experiments, conducted across various datasets and model designs, reveal a positive relationship between the difficulties of the underlying adaptation problem and the sample complexity of the meta model. When it comes to leveraging multilingual training data for monolingual translation tasks, prior research suggests that a small portion of it is sufficient. Nonetheless, utilizing only a fraction of the data comes with the drawback of increased uncertainty and instability in the model. This issue could be addressed by reducing either the model's weights or the input embeddings, with quantization offering a method to achieve this. We compare the efficacy of quantization and feature extraction in low-resource machine translation models, with a specific focus on their impact on model propensity for mode mode collapse, which in turn affects a model's ability to generalize. We find that while quantization improves a model's generalization performance, it increases its sensitivity to hyperparameter selection. On the other hand, feature extraction results in improved generalization while reducing a model's susceptibility to hyperparameter instability. Finally, we investigate the feasibility of leveraging pre-trained translation models for our task and find that while they demonstrate weaker performance, it may still be a viable option when no high-resource translation data is available. We observe that low-resource data pre-training, in conjunction with decoupling the embedding layer, enables the attainment of comparable results comparable to those achieved through post-distillation extraction of features. Ultimately, our research reveals that feature extraction offers the more stable and efficient approach for developing lightweight low-resource MT models. This finding holds particularly true when a substantial fraction of high-quality training data is not accessible. It suggests that early feature extraction could be a more reliable technique for achieving state-of-the-art MT performance in data-scarce environments. Moreover, given its relatively low impact on model generalization performance, it makes it a more attractive option compared to quantization. We propose that to optimize the extraction of features for low-resource MT, a model's architecture should be designed with decoupling in mind as the default. This way, even when a small portion of the data is all that's available, a model's ability to generalize effectively will not be compromised. We provide a detailed set of best practices for achieving state-of-the-art low-resource MT using decoupling in your architecture. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the benefits and drawbacks of prioritizing generalization performance versus hyperparameter stability. Ultimately, it aims to contribute to the development of efficient and robust low-resource MT systems. In the medical field, state-of-the-art computerized image processing relies heavily on deep learning, yet gathering sufficient labeled data for training remains a significant challenge. A major issue arises during the detection and quantification of rare medical conditions, such as certain types of pneumonia, due to their relatively rare occurrence. Research has shown that data augmentation is a viable method to overcome this limitation, but its application is still debated. This paper explores the potential of combining state-of-the-art image enhancement techniques, specifically depth-wise separable convolution and contrast enhancement, with data augmentation to reduce the need for labeled data in the context of pneumonia segmentation. Using the CHAOS dataset for our study, we evaluated the performance of four different models: a model with standard augmentation but without image enhancement, a model with image enhancement but no standard augmentation, a model with both standard augmentation and image enhancement, and a model with standard augmentation alone. Our findings suggest that the model with standard augmentation alone performed best, indicating that data augmentation can be an effective tool in this context. However, when we applied our best model to a smaller subset of the CHAOS dataset comprising only ten labeled images, we observed improved performance compared to a model with standard augmentation alone. Increasing the influence of depth-wise separable convolution and contrast enhancement in our model further, we were able to reduce the labeled data requirement to six images while maintaining the same level of performance. This research aimed to reduce the necessity for labeled data during the training of a segmentation model, and through our experiments, we were able to achieve this goal by utilizing image enhancement techniques. These findings could have significant implications for the medical community, given the substantial costs associated with collecting and labeling large datasets. By leveraging image enhancement techniques to reduce the labeled data requirement, we could increase accessibility to deep learning tools and resources, ultimately contributing to the advancement of medical image processing.

Recent breakthroughs in large language models have led to remarkable progress in image description tasks through the use of pre-trained models. However, the captured descriptions often lack diversity in style, leading to descriptive repetition under varying image content. This research explores the potential of prompt engineering and model fine-tuning as an effective approach to developing personalized image description models that can capture both task-specific details and image content. We demonstrate this method's efficacy by successfully customizing a pre-trained, generic image description model to achieve state-of-the-art results on the MS-COCO dataset. Furthermore, the resulting model's descriptive output displays both increased diversity in style and a clearer understanding of the image content. This study validates the capability of prompt engineering and model fine-tuning to develop tailored language models for specific tasks. It also highlights the importance of prompts in both model adaptation and objective definition. In addition, our study reveals the significant impact of model parameters on the quality of prompts and, by extension, the quality of the model itself. Ultimately, these findings establish the foundation for the development of a regulatory framework governing the use of language model prompts, enabling the creation of a prompt market where developers can source and utilize prompts effectively while addressing task-specific requirements. Intervening in complex systems frequently yields unintended consequences, often stemming from subtle alterations and unpredictable interactions among variables. To identify potential causes of harm, we developed and applied a causal analysis framework, which seeks to answer three key questions: What are the potential adverse outcomes? What actions could cause such harm? What measures can be taken to prevent it? Through this comprehensive analysis, our goal is to gain a deeper understanding of the causal relationships at play. To test the robustness and versatility of the framework, our case study focuses on the potential for damage in the game of Tetris. By leveraging available game data, we were able to derive a probabilistic model representing the Tetris game state, which enabled us to identify and analyze various counterfactual scenarios. By applying the causal analysis framework to Tetris, we were able to identify a range of possible harms, understand their causes, and explore alternative strategies to prevent them. Ultimately, our results highlight the value of utilizing causal analysis techniques to identify and mitigate potential risks in complex systems. Given the limitations of the available Tetris data, our findings serve as a model for how such an approach could be effectively applied in real-world scenarios where the mechanisms are poorly understood. Recent advancements in end-to-end speech-to-text models have greatly impacted our daily lives, but a critical limitation persists: they can only operate in languages for which there is substantial training data. As a result, using voice-based translation in languages with limited data is often unfeasible or produces poor outcomes. In this research, we investigate a novel challenge: translating spoken language into spoken language without any training data from the same speaker. To tackle this problem, we draw upon the ability of generative text-to-text models to translate speech into speech across languages and develop a text-to-text approach for speech input. By leveraging a generative speech model to convert written text into speech, we can integrate it with the text-to-text model to achieve zero-shot voice translation. Through a comprehensive evaluation, we test our proposed method on three language pairs: English to English, English to German, and English to Mandarin. Our model achieves a reasonable level of accuracy in translation, especially when speaker-independent non-attention generative speech models are used. Furthermore, we found that our model can also perform well on two other languages, namely Dutch and Russian, despite these languages not being directly involved in the evaluation process. Ultimately, our model sets the stage for future advancements in zero-shot voice translation and multiple voice translation. The source code and model checkpoints for this research can be accessed at the provided GitHub repository. The results of our model have also been made available through a GitHub repository containing the model outputs. This work extends the capabilities of voice-to-text models, enabling zero-shot voice translation and laying the groundwork for future breakthroughs in this area. In a related development, it is worth noting that our model's results indicate it is possible to translate German to Mandarin, a language for which there is very limited data available, and this represents an important development in the field of voice-based translation. To take this research forward, it would be beneficial to test the application of our model to other languages, and potentially integrate it with other techniques, such as actuated voice translation. Building on these findings, a potential next step could be to develop a voice-based translation model that is entirely within the speech domain. This goal is particularly significant, given that some individuals may experience difficulties with spoken languages due to conditions such as stuttering or other speech disorders. Ultimately, it is our hope that this research will contribute to the development of speech translation tools that are accessible to a wider audience, and that it will inspire further breakthroughs in this area. The models developed during this research are available for others to build upon

This work extends the work on generalized heat conduction equations as initially explored by Coleman and Gurtin, incorporating boundary conditions that factor in internal heat sources and volume changes. The study covers basic heat conduction with or without memory, along with non-standard scenarios, all of which are analyzed within a bounded area and a cylindrical domain with a dynamic boundary. The results are then translated into practical applications, resulting in a system of equations that must be solved in conjunction with boundary conditions that depend on the volume and time derivative of the boundary temperature. This system consists of a nonlinear partial differential equation, an equation for the volume rate, and three boundary conditions, forming a closed system. The study demonstrates the uniqueness of the solutions and their continuity, and we present various examples of specific cases. A critical aspect of this system lies in its thermodynamic consistency and the resulting energy inequality, which is a necessary and sufficient condition for the solutions to be valid. The local well-ordering of the system enables numerical solutions to be developed, which in turn facilitates a comprehensive analysis of the long-term behavior of the thermal profiles. This is particularly evident in the examples of periodic heat transport and long-term equilibrium scenarios, which demonstrate the significance of the memory function and the volume changes on the behavior of the thermal profiles. Lastly, a comparison with the standard heat conduction equations highlights the inherent differences between the various systems, with the standard heat equation being a particular case of the more general systems under certain conditions. These general conditions are satisfied in the examples presented, which include a comparison between standard and generalized heat conduction. By applying these concepts to the study of laser-induced phase transitions, we demonstrate that the thermodynamic consistency of the system plays a pivotal role in the results, with the thermally activated transitions displaying a distinctive time-dependent behavior at the boundary levels. The study also reveals that the volume changes triggered by the internal heat sources and the dynamic boundary conditions do not exert a significant influence on the long-term thermodynamic properties, which are determined by the thermodynamic properties of the individual materials in contact. These results are demonstrated in the examples presented and are a direct consequence of the validity of the thermodynamic consistency of the system. Accurate low voltage network load forecasting is crucial to support the effective operation of the distributed energy delivery. However, the high level of unobserved load points hinders the quality of state-of-the-art forecasting methods grounded in measurement data. Integration of external knowledge, particularly daily peak forecasts provided by distribution operators, offers an effective means to overcome these limitations. This research utilizes a probabilistic approach to predict low voltage network loads, combining measurement data with a peak forecast to estimate daily load curves. A stochastic elimination technique is used in conjunction with a state-space model based measurement update to correctly incorporate external peak forecasts into measurement data-driven load predictions. Notably, our proposed approach demonstrates improved performance compared to established forecasting techniques, particularly in networks with limited measurement data. Furthermore, our method effectively utilizes daily peak forecasts, resulting in enhanced overall forecasting accuracy. A comprehensive evaluation on a real-world dataset has been conducted to support the reliability of our findings. To address the issue of detection tools for COVID-19 being biased due to prior health knowledge, we conducted experiments using chest CT scans and found that current methods still perform poorly in areas with fewer cases. We therefore developed a new learning method called WGL, which utilizes weak object label annotations for both localization and segmentation tasks. By employing multi-task learning with noise regularization, our approach can accurately identify objects even with limited data. We tested this model with various datasets and customization options and found that it performs consistently better than the current standard approaches. Moreover, our results suggest that the WGL method is capable of producing robust estimates that are comparable to pandemic-level performance, indicating its potential as an unbiased diagnostic tool. We have made the source code available to facilitate future research. Ultimately, our study highlights the importance of object representation learning for health challenges like the COVID-19 pandemic. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ResearchIan/WGL.

A novel spinal CT segmentation framework is introduced to streamline the spinal column visualization process. This system is comprised of two core components: a spine rectification method leveraging spine path estimation and anatomically-controlled shape optimization, which work in tandem to identify and define vertebral body boundaries. The initial step of spine path estimation enables subsequent segmentation, while error accumulation is minimized due to spine's relatively fixed anatomical position. Evaluation with 100 subjects demonstrated high precision vertebral body segmentation, with notable results including 100% accuracy in vertebral body localization across all levels and Seg-Dice scores reaching 0.96 for T7-L5. Furthermore, this framework's segmentation results compared favorably to state-of-the-art methods, with significant time efficiencies also being observed. In fact, the automatic segmentation process took only 137.2 milliseconds per slice, an impressive rate of at least three times faster than other top-performing methods. Ultimately, this spinal CT segmentation framework boasts exceptional precision and efficiency while accommodating a wide variety of anatomical structures, making it beneficial for rapid spinal column visualization in clinical settings. With notable segmentation results and relatively low computational demands across a broad spectrum of subjects with normal, osteoporotic, and tumor-based spinal anomalies, this method's adaptability and clinical applications are considerable. In the quantum mechanics of light-matter interaction, intense electromagnetic fields play a significant role. USTLC physics, characterized by substantial energy exchange between light and matter, is distinguished by its extreme coupling, exceeding the natural frequency of particles. This field can be amplified by reflection, reaching values far exceeding the surrounding vacuum's Cohernent Off Shell Field, a phenomenon known as super-Kerr effect. In an investigation into this field's impact, we studied electron collisions within a cavity, revealing a novel stabilization effect. This USTLC phenomenon is marked by the stabilization of electron orbits through vacuum oscillations resulting from self-induced potentials. Moreover, we observed a resonance shift, a first-order USTLC effect, characterized by the energy optimization of electron orbits via coherent amplification. Notably, this USTLC effect is observable in particle scattering, a method facilitating the exploration of strong light-matter coupling. Additionally, we have proposed an experimental approach based on x-ray scattering using novel materials with frequencies matched to x-ray wavelengths. Consequently, we have demonstrated that, through vacuum oscillations and resonance, it is feasible to achieve stable orbits in intense electromagnetic fields, a development opening new avenues to exploring strong light-matter coupling. The associated instability and novel resonance effects can be leveraged to enhance particle interaction, a range of phenomena expanding current understanding of light-matter coupling and the microphysics of scattering processes. Moreover, this USTLC effect may be utilized to increase coherence in previously unstable processes, a potential breakthrough for future high-energy particle physics. A fundamental goal in fashion image retrieval involves extracting vital characteristics from abundant image data to meet user needs for finding similar or diverse fashion items. Manipulating key features is a crucial approach for understanding a image's intrinsic properties. The challenge lies in altering a specific attribute while ignoring others, particularly in the context of fashion images where images are densely connected. Prior methods relied on supervised learning, ineffective against unseen data. We propose a semi-unsupervised, federated learning model that identifies prominent features and adapts these to meet fashion industry needs. By doing so, it trains a versatile model using a modest number of labeled images and a vast number of unlabeled images. We present two novel federated learning methods to make our model resilient to style fluctuations in the fashion industry. We evaluate our approach through both objective and subjective measures, comparing the manipulated images to human judgments on what constitutes similar fashion items. The results demonstrate that our model performs better than a range of baselines with less robust results and a more compact model with reduced computational requirements. We derive effective low-energy actions for gravity on manifolds with curved geometry by incorporating higher-derivative terms.  By employing Double Field Theory and the star product, we investigate actions governed by twisted differential operators.  In this context, we explore general metrics and explore alternative theories of gravity that diverge from General Relativity, with a focus on violations of the Riemannian hypothesis and energies below the Planck threshold.  Our results are validated for two-dimensional and three-dimensional manifolds, with the possibility of extending these principles to higher dimensions.  Finally, we briefly outline the application of these principles to strings and heterotic strings in higher dimensions.  Nevertheless, we note that higher-dimensional cases are still lacking in our derivation.  A crucial element in the construction would be the creation of a metric with a non-constant $\theta^{\ast n}$ transformation, with the potential for forming more complex metrics via the resolution of the Fourier transform.  Such a approach could reveal the form of the higher-derivative action for these more complex metrics.  An illustration of this can be seen in the example of a torus in two dimensions, where we generate a time-dependent metric with a constant $\theta^{\ast n}$ transformation.  Although this example does not fully comply with the requirements for the higher-derivative action, we can obtain a approximate solution by setting the time-dependent component to zero.  Therefore, we can derive the two-dimensional action for this case.  An alternative method for obtaining the higher-derivative action in higher dimensions would be to relax the requirement of the non-constant $\theta^{\ast n}$ transformation.  By setting the off-diagonal components of the metric to zero, we can derive the higher-derivative action for any dimension.
